title: How seeds travel: wings and wind, water, animals and people, and why people save seeds

summary.text: A tree cannot walk, yet young trees of its kind appear across a valley and on far islands. How do its seeds get there? In this unit you will test paper winged seeds in the wind of a fan, see where 30 drops of one spinner land, and trace where ten foods came from.
summary.art: A tall tree on a hillside with winged seeds drifting sideways from the top branches across a valley, a coconut floating on the sea below, a hornbill flying with a fruit, and a woman holding a clay pot of seeds.

intro.hook: A plate of idli and sambar looks as South Indian as food can be. But the tomato and the chilli in the sambar came from the Americas, about 500 years ago. The tamarind came from Africa, long before that. The onion came from Central Asia. None of these plants can walk. So how did their seeds reach your kitchen?
intro.text: Every seed has to leave the parent plant somehow. Some seeds have wings. Some float. Some are swallowed, and some are thrown. Some ride with people. In this unit you first read the shapes of seeds from your kitchen, and guess how each one travels. Then you build three paper fliers and test them in front of a fan. The result tells you what a wing really does. After that you follow the longest journeys of all, and meet the people who save seeds.
intro.art: A steel plate of idli and sambar on a table, with thin dotted lines running from the tomato, the chilli, the tamarind and the onion to four small outline maps of far-away lands.

outcomes: I can give two reasons why a seed often does better away from the parent plant.
I can look at a fruit or a seed and say how they probably travel, and give my evidence.
I can explain how a wing or a tuft of hairs slows a fall, using weight and air resistance.
I can explain that the wind carries a winged seed, and that the distance depends on time in the air, wind speed and height.
I can run a fair test with repeated tries and a mean, and say what my results show.
I can describe a seed shadow, and say why the few seeds that go far matter so much.
I can give examples of people carrying seeds across the world, and say what changed because of it.
I can explain why people save many varieties of seeds, and describe two ways of saving them.

terms.meaning: Seed dispersal is the movement of seeds away from the parent plant. To disperse means to spread out in different directions.
terms.example: The seeds of a peepal tree are dispersed by birds, who eat the figs and drop the seeds far away.
terms.art: A tree with arrows going outwards in all directions, each arrow ending in a small seed.

terms.meaning: A fruit is the part of a plant that grows from the ovary of a flower and holds the seeds. Many fruits are built to help the seeds travel.
terms.example: A drumstick, a coconut, a tamarind pod and a chilli are all fruits.
terms.art: A drumstick, a coconut, a tamarind pod and a red chilli in a row, each cut open to show the seeds.

terms.meaning: Competition happens when living beings need the same thing and there is not enough for all. Plants compete for light, water and space.
terms.example: A hundred mango seedlings under one mango tree compete for the little light that reaches the ground.
terms.art: Many thin seedlings crowded in the dark shade under a big tree, and one sturdy seedling standing in sunlight farther away.

terms.meaning: Air resistance is the push of air against anything that moves through the air. Scientists also call this push drag. A wider and faster thing meets more drag.
terms.example: A flat sheet of paper falls slowly because of drag. The same sheet crushed into a ball falls fast.
terms.art: A flat sheet of paper and a paper ball falling side by side, with many small arrows pushing up under the sheet and few under the ball.

terms.meaning: The steady fall speed is the speed at which a falling thing stops speeding up. At this speed, the drag pushing up is equal to the weight pulling down. Scientists call this speed terminal velocity.
terms.example: A spinning mahogany seed reaches a steady fall speed of about one metre each second.
terms.art: A spinning winged seed with one arrow pointing down marked weight and one equal arrow pointing up marked drag.

terms.meaning: A samara is a dry fruit with a thin, papery wing. The wing grew from the wall of the fruit.
terms.example: The flat, round fruit of the Indian elm is a samara. So is the spinning fruit of a maple tree.
terms.art: A round papery Indian elm fruit with the seed in the middle, beside a one-winged maple fruit.

terms.meaning: Autorotation is spinning that is caused only by falling through the air. No engine or muscle turns the wing.
terms.example: A mahogany seed starts to spin after falling a short way, and then comes down slowly like a small helicopter.
terms.art: A one-winged seed falling, with a curved arrow showing the spin and a dotted spiral showing the path.

terms.meaning: A pappus is a tuft of fine hairs on top of a small dry fruit. The hairs act like a parachute.
terms.example: The fluffy white balls on the roadside weed tridax are made of hundreds of fruits, each with a pappus.
terms.art: One tridax fruit drawn large: a thin dark fruit below and a ring of feathery white hairs above.

terms.meaning: A vortex is air or water that spins round and round, like the water going down a drain.
terms.example: A small vortex of air sits on top of a spinning maple seed and helps to hold the seed up.
terms.art: A spinning winged seed seen from the side with a small swirl of air drawn just above the front edge of the wing.

terms.meaning: A seed shadow is the pattern of places where the seeds of one plant land. Most seeds land near the parent, and a few land far away.
terms.example: Under and around one neem tree the ground is thick with fallen seeds. Fifty metres away there are only a few.
terms.art: A tree seen from above with many dots close to the trunk, fewer dots farther out, and three lonely dots far away.

terms.meaning: Long-distance dispersal is the rare journey of a seed that travels very much farther than most seeds of that plant.
terms.example: A coconut that floats from one island to another has made a long-distance journey.
terms.art: A map of sea and two islands with a dotted line and a small coconut travelling between them.

terms.meaning: A frugivore is an animal who eats mostly fruit. Many frugivores swallow seeds and drop them somewhere else.
terms.example: Hornbills, bulbuls, barbets, fruit bats and civets are frugivores.
terms.art: A great hornbill on a branch holding a fig in the tip of a long curved beak.

terms.meaning: An elaiosome is a small, oily food parcel on the outside of some seeds. Ants carry the whole seed home to eat the parcel.
terms.example: A castor seed has a pale bump at one end. That bump is an elaiosome.
terms.art: A shiny patterned castor seed with a pale bump at one end, being carried by a black ant.

terms.meaning: In explosive dispersal the fruit itself throws the seeds. The drying or swelling fruit stores energy like a bent spring, and then lets go suddenly.
terms.example: A ripe balsam pod curls up at a touch and flings the seeds out.
terms.art: A green balsam pod bursting open, with its walls curled into coils and small seeds flying outwards.

terms.meaning: A propagule is any part of a plant that can leave the parent and grow into a new plant. A seed is one kind of propagule.
terms.example: A mangrove tree drops long green seedlings that have already sprouted. Each one is a propagule.
terms.art: A mangrove branch with long green pencil-shaped seedlings hanging down, and one floating upright in the water below.

terms.meaning: Domestication is the slow change of a wild plant or animal into one that lives with people and depends on them. People cause the change by choosing which ones to grow or breed.
terms.example: Farmed paddy was domesticated from wild rice over thousands of years.
terms.art: A thin stalk of wild rice with a few grains falling off, beside a heavy head of farmed paddy with every grain still attached.

terms.meaning: Shattering is the way a wild grass drops ripe grains from the stalk, one by one. Farmed grains have mostly lost this habit.
terms.example: Wild rice shatters, so the grain falls into the water. Farmed paddy holds the grain until someone threshes the stalks.
terms.art: A hand brushing a wild rice stalk so that grains fall, and a second hand brushing a paddy stalk where the grains stay on.

terms.meaning: A variety is one kind within a crop, such as one kind of rice. A landrace is an old variety that farmers in one place have grown and saved for many generations.
terms.example: Mappillai samba, kattuyanam and navara are old rice landraces of Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
terms.art: Five small heaps of rice grains of different colours and shapes on a banana leaf: red, black, long, short and round.

terms.meaning: A seed bank is a place where seeds of many kinds and varieties are kept alive for the future. Most seed banks keep the seeds dry and cold.
terms.example: The National Genebank in New Delhi keeps more than four lakh seed samples.
terms.art: A cold room with shelves of labelled sealed packets, and a person in a thick jacket holding one packet.

terms.meaning: An invasive species is a living being who was carried to a new place, spreads fast there, and crowds out the beings who lived there before.
terms.example: Lantana was brought to India as a garden plant about 200 years ago. Now lantana covers large parts of many forests.
terms.art: A forest floor covered with lantana bushes in flower, with a bulbul eating the dark berries.

explanations.definition: Seed dispersal is the movement of seeds away from the parent plant. A seed that lands away from the parent often has a better chance to live.
explanations.description: A plant makes many seeds. If all of them fell straight down, they would sprout in a heap under the parent. There are three reasons why that is a poor start. The first is competition. The seedlings would need the same light, water and space as each other and as the parent, and the parent's leaves already shade the ground. The second is enemies. The insects and moulds that feed on one kind of plant gather where that plant is common. Seedlings near the parent meet more of them. Two scientists, Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell, proposed this around 1970. Studies in many forests have since found that seedlings close to a parent of the same kind die more often. It is not true for every tree. The third reason is change. A place that is good today may flood, burn or dry out. A plant whose seeds reach many places is more likely to have some young who live. Leaving home is also risky. Most seeds that travel land somewhere bad. Dispersal is worth it only because a few land somewhere good.
examples: Under a big mango tree you may find dozens of mango seedlings after the rains. Almost none of them become trees.
A banyan seed dropped by a bird on a far wall has no banyan above to shade them.
A groundnut plant is an exception. The plant pushes the young pods into the soil right beside the parent.
explanations.art: A big tree with a crowd of small weak seedlings in the shade below, insects on their leaves, and one healthy seedling growing in a sunny gap far to the side.

explanations.concept: Reading a fruit: the shape shows how the seeds travel
explanations.definition: A fruit is the part of a plant that holds the seeds. The shape, weight and covering of a fruit are evidence of how the seeds usually leave.
explanations.description: You can often work out how a seed travels by looking closely. A thin wing or a tuft of hair means wind. The seed is light and has a wide surface for the air to push on. A thick, light, waterproof husk full of air means water. Soft, sweet, brightly coloured flesh round hard seeds means that an animal eats the fruit. The animal digests the flesh and drops the seeds. Hooks or sticky gum mean that the fruit clings to fur, feathers or clothes. A dry pod that curls or snaps open means that the plant throws the seeds. A small oily bump on a seed is food for ants, who carry the seed home. Many plants use two ways, one after the other. A castor pod throws the seeds, and then ants carry them farther. A shape is good evidence, but it is not proof. To be sure, scientists watch what really happens to the seeds.
examples: A drumstick seed has three papery wings, so the wind can carry them.
A coconut has a thick husk of fibres with air between them, so the coconut floats.
Spear grass seeds have sharp points that catch in socks and in the fur of dogs and cattle.
A ripe tomato is soft, red and juicy, with small slippery seeds that pass through an animal unharmed.
explanations.art: Six small pictures in a grid: a winged seed in the wind, a husked coconut on water, a bird eating a berry, a hooked burr on a sock, a pod bursting, and an ant carrying a seed.

explanations.concept: How a wing slows a fall
explanations.definition: Air resistance, or drag, is the push of air against a moving thing. A falling seed speeds up until the drag pushing up is equal to the weight pulling down. From then on the seed falls at a steady speed.
explanations.description: When a seed is let go, the Earth pulls the seed down. This pull is the seed's weight. At first the seed falls faster and faster. But a falling thing has to push air out of the way, and the air pushes back. That push is drag. Drag gets bigger as the speed gets bigger. So there comes a speed at which the drag is as big as the weight. The two pushes cancel, and the seed stops speeding up. This is the steady fall speed. A wing changes this speed. A wing adds a lot of surface and very little weight. With more surface, the air pushes back harder at any speed. So the drag matches the weight at a much lower speed. A packed seed with no wing may fall at 5 metres each second or more. A winged seed of the same weight may fall at 1 metre each second. Scientists compare seeds by how much weight each square centimetre of wing must hold up. They call this the wing loading. A lower wing loading gives a slower fall.
examples: A flat sheet of paper and the same sheet crushed into a ball weigh the same. The flat sheet falls far more slowly.
A mahogany seed with the wing broken off drops like a small stone.
A person under an open parachute falls at about 5 metres each second, slow enough to land safely.
explanations.art: Two falling seeds side by side: a packed one with a long down arrow for weight and a short up arrow for drag, and a winged one with the two arrows equal.

explanations.concept: The spinning seed: a wing that makes a small whirl of air
explanations.definition: Autorotation is spinning caused only by falling through the air. A spinning winged seed falls more slowly than the same seed would fall without spinning.
explanations.description: A mahogany seed has one long wing with the heavy seed at one end. After falling a short way, the seed starts to spin. The heavy end stays near the centre, and the wing sweeps round like one blade of a helicopter. Why does spinning help? As the wing sweeps round, it meets far more air each second than a wing that only drops. In 2009, David Lentink and his team studied model maple seeds in a tank of oil. They found a small whirl of air sitting on top of the front edge of the spinning wing. A whirl like this is called a leading-edge vortex. The air pressure inside the whirl is low, so the air below the wing pushes the wing up harder. This whirl lets the wing make much more lift than a wing of that size otherwise could. Insects, bats and hummingbirds get extra lift from the same kind of whirl when they hover. The seed has no muscles. The fall itself turns the wing.
examples: Mahogany trees along many city roads in India drop one-winged seeds that spin all the way down.
Sal fruits in the forests of central and eastern India have wings that grew from the sepals of the flower.
The fruit of the vine called hiptage, or madhavi lata, has three wings and spins as it falls.
explanations.art: A one-winged mahogany seed spinning, drawn from the side, with a small swirl of air above the front edge of the wing and an arrow marked lift pointing up.

explanations.definition: A pappus is a tuft of fine hairs on a small dry fruit. The hairs slow the fall, as a parachute does.
explanations.description: Look at the fluffy white ball on a tridax plant by the roadside. Each tiny fruit has a ring of feathery hairs on top. A dandelion fruit has about 100 hairs. The hairs cover less than a tenth of the circle they spread across. The rest is gaps. You might expect the air to rush through the gaps. It does not. Each hair is so thin that the air close to it is slowed down. The slowed air round one hair overlaps with the slowed air round the next. So the tuft acts almost like a solid disc, but weighs far less. In 2018, Cathal Cummins, Naomi Nakayama and their team in Edinburgh filmed dandelion fruits in a small wind tunnel. They found a ring-shaped whirl of air floating just above the hairs. Nobody had seen a whirl of that kind before. It adds to the drag and keeps the fruit steady. A dandelion fruit falls at only about 30 to 40 centimetres each second.
examples: Tridax, a small daisy with a white and yellow flower, grows on almost every roadside in India.
A ripe pod of calotropis, called erukku or aak, splits and lets out flat brown seeds with long silky hairs.
The floss of the silk cotton tree drifts across towns in the hot weeks before the monsoon, carrying the seeds.
explanations.art: A single dandelion fruit drawn large, falling, with a ring-shaped swirl of air drawn just above the tuft of hairs.

explanations.definition: A winged or tufted seed has no way to push forward. The moving air carries the seed sideways while the seed falls. The longer the fall lasts and the faster the wind, the farther the seed goes.
explanations.description: People say that winged seeds fly. But a seed has no engine and no muscles. If you drop a winged seed in still air, the seed comes straight down. All the sideways travel comes from the wind. A wing helps in two ways, and both come from the same cause. The wing gives the air a lot to push on, compared with the weight. First, the seed falls slowly, so the wind has longer to carry the seed. Second, the wind sweeps a broad, light seed up to the wind's own speed very quickly. A rough rule follows. Distance is about the time in the air multiplied by the speed of the wind. A seed that falls for 20 seconds in a wind of 5 metres each second lands about 100 metres away. So three things make a seed go far: a slow fall, a strong wind, and a high start. This is one reason why tall trees can use wings well. Rising air matters too. On a hot afternoon, air rises from warm ground. A few seeds are caught in rising air and lifted high above the trees. Those few may travel many kilometres.
examples: A seed let go from 20 metres falls for 20 seconds at a steady 1 metre each second. From 2 metres the fall lasts only 2 seconds.
Orchid seeds are as fine as dust. They fall so slowly that the wind can carry them for hundreds of kilometres.
Many trees with winged seeds drop them in the dry, windy season, when the leaves are off and the wind passes through.
explanations.art: A tall tree and a short bush in the same wind, each letting go one winged seed, with a long slanting path from the tree and a short one from the bush.

explanations.concept: The seed shadow: most land near, a few go far
explanations.definition: A seed shadow is the pattern of places where the seeds of one plant land. In almost every plant, most seeds land close to the parent and a few land far away.
explanations.description: Drop the same paper spinner many times in the same wind, and the landing places differ. The wind is never perfectly steady. For a real tree the spread is much wider. Most seeds leave on an ordinary breeze and land within a few tree-heights. A few leave in a strong gust, or are lifted by rising air, and go very far. If you counted the seeds at each distance, the count would be high near the tree. It would drop quickly and then tail off slowly over a long distance. The far end of this pattern is very hard to measure, because one seed in ten thousand is nearly impossible to find. Yet those rare seeds matter most for where a kind of plant can live. Here is the evidence. About 12,000 years ago the ice that covered northern Europe melted. Oak trees then spread north by about 1,000 kilometres in a few thousand years. An acorn falls only a few metres from the oak. In 1899 the British botanist Clement Reid worked out that falling acorns alone would need about a million years to cover that distance. The answer is rare long trips. Birds called jays carry acorns for kilometres and bury them.
examples: Under a rain tree the ground is covered in pods. A hundred metres away you find only one or two.
A new island of sand in a river grows grass and bushes within a few years, from seeds that came on wind, water and birds.
Peepal seedlings sprout on high walls and temple towers, far from any peepal tree.
explanations.art: A bar chart drawn as columns of seeds: a tall column close to a tree, shorter and shorter columns farther away, and one single seed very far to the right.

explanations.definition: Some fruits and seeds float, and are carried by rivers, floods and the sea. A floating fruit has trapped air and a covering that keeps water out.
explanations.description: A coconut is built for the sea. The outer skin is smooth and waterproof. Under the skin is a thick husk of fibres with air between them, so the whole fruit floats high. Inside the hard shell, the seed has food and water for the journey. In one small test of 15 coconuts, most were still able to sprout after floating in sea water for 110 days. In that time a slow ocean current can carry a coconut a few thousand kilometres. Mangrove trees do something different. The seed sprouts while still hanging on the mother tree, and grows into a long green seedling. This is called vivipary, which means live birth. The seedling then drops into the water and floats away on the tide, often lying flat at first. Later the root end takes in water and sinks, and the seedling roots in the mud. Fresh water carries seeds too. Lotus fruits and the seeds of many riverbank trees float downstream in the monsoon.
examples: Coconut palms line the coasts of Kerala, Lakshadweep and the Andaman Islands.
At Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu and in the Sundarbans of Bengal, mangrove seedlings hang from the trees like green pencils.
The Indian almond tree, common on beaches and city roads, has a corky fruit that floats in the sea.
explanations.art: A coconut cut in half to show the skin, the thick fibre husk, the shell and the seed inside, floating on sea water.

explanations.definition: Many plants are dispersed by animals. Some seeds are carried inside an animal who ate the fruit. Others are carried on the outside, or carried away to be stored as food.
explanations.description: A sweet fruit is a payment. The plant spends sugar on the flesh, and the animal who eats the flesh carries the seeds away. The seeds are hard or slippery, so many pass through the gut whole. They land in a dropping, which is a small heap of manure. Unripe fruit is green, hard and sour, because the seeds inside are not ready. Chillies show how exact this can be. In 2001, Joshua Tewksbury and Gary Nabhan tested wild chillies. Birds ate the hot fruit freely, and the seeds passed through them and sprouted well. Mice and rats tasted the heat and left the fruit alone. When they did eat mild chillies, they chewed the seeds, and no seeds sprouted. Birds do not sense the hot chemical, which is called capsaicin. So the heat keeps seed-chewers away and lets seed-carriers eat. Large animals carry large seeds. In the forests of Arunachal Pradesh, the scientist Aparajita Datta followed hornbills for years. She showed that hornbills swallow big fruits whole and drop the seeds far away, often kilometres from the parent tree. Elephants carry mango, jackfruit and wood apple seeds, and leave them in a great heap of dung. Other seeds ride outside, with hooks that catch in fur. Ants carry seeds that have an oily food parcel.
examples: A bulbul eats lantana berries and drops the seeds from a perch somewhere else.
Flying foxes, the big fruit bats, carry figs and Indian almonds away from the tree and drop the seeds below their feeding perch.
Flowerpeckers eat the sticky berries of a plant that grows on mango branches. They wipe the gluey seed onto another branch, where the seed sprouts.
A squirrel buries nuts to eat later and forgets some. The forgotten ones can sprout.
explanations.art: A great hornbill in flight over a forest with a fruit in the beak, and below, a seedling growing from a dropped seed far from a large fruiting tree.

explanations.definition: In explosive dispersal the fruit throws the seeds. The fruit stores energy as it dries or swells, in the way a bent spring stores energy, and then lets go all at once.
explanations.description: A ripe balsam pod is under strain. The outer layer of the pod wall is swollen with water and is trying to get longer. The inner layer holds it back. The five strips of the wall are joined along weak seams. A touch breaks a seam. Each strip then curls up in a few thousandths of a second and flings the seeds out. Other pods store energy by drying. The wall of a bauhinia pod has two layers of stiff fibres. The fibres in one layer run at a slant to the fibres in the other. When the pod dries, each layer shrinks in a different direction. The two halves cannot both shrink flat, so they twist into spirals. Shahaf Armon and her team in Jerusalem worked this out in 2011, using strips of stretched rubber. The pods of the rubber tree split with a loud crack and throw the seeds more than ten metres. Throwing is a short trip compared with wind or birds. But throwing costs the plant no sweet flesh, and needs no partner.
examples: Balsam is grown in many Indian gardens. Children press the ripe pods to make them pop.
The dry pods of the cracker plant, a small purple-flowered weed, burst when a raindrop wets them.
Castor capsules dry and snap open in the sun, and the seeds fly out.
explanations.art: A balsam pod in three stages: closed and fat, splitting along the seams, and with the five strips curled into tight coils as seeds fly away.

explanations.concept: Big seed or far seed: a plant has one budget
explanations.definition: A plant has a limited amount of food to spend on seeds. The plant can make a few large seeds with a big food store, or very many small seeds with almost none.
explanations.description: A large seed gives the seedling a strong start. The seedling can grow tall roots and leaves in shade or in dry soil before the food runs out. But a large seed is heavy. Wind cannot lift a seed like that. Only a large animal or water can carry one. A small seed can be carried by a breath of wind, and the plant can make thousands. But each seedling has almost nothing to live on, and must land in just the right place. So there is no best size. The largest seed in the world is the coco de mer, a palm of the Seychelles islands. One seed can weigh more than 15 kilograms. The fresh fruit sinks in the sea, and these palms grow wild on only two islands. The smallest seeds belong to orchids. One orchid pod can hold more than a million seeds. An orchid seed has no food store at all. The seed can only sprout if a fungus in the soil feeds the seedling at first.
examples: One coconut palm makes about 50 to 100 large seeds in a year.
One tridax plant makes thousands of tiny seeds in a year.
A mango seedling can live for weeks in deep shade on the food in the large seed.
explanations.art: A balance scale with one huge double-lobed coco de mer seed on one pan and a heap of dust-fine orchid seeds on the other.

explanations.definition: People carry seeds farther and faster than wind, water or any other animal. People carry crops on purpose, and weeds by accident. Domestication has changed some crops so much that they can no longer disperse without us.
explanations.description: Humans are animals who carry seeds, as hornbills and elephants do. But we carry them across oceans. After 1492, ships began to sail between the Americas and the rest of the world. Portuguese ships reached India in 1498. Within about a hundred years they had brought chilli, and later potato, tomato, maize, groundnut, papaya, guava, cashew, pineapple and tapioca. Before that, Indian cooks made food hot with black pepper and long pepper. Seeds went the other way too. Pepper, mango and sugarcane left Asia for the rest of the world. We carry seeds by accident as well. Seeds ride in grain sacks, in soil, on tyres and on shoes. The weed parthenium probably reached India mixed in wheat that came by ship from America in the 1950s. Tridax, the roadside daisy, also came from the Americas. Some of these newcomers spread fast and crowd out the plants who lived there before. They are called invasive species. The oldest change is in our crops. Wild rice shatters, which means the ripe grains drop off one by one. Early farmers could only harvest the grains that stayed on the stalk. Those were the grains they sowed the next year. After many generations, almost every plant in the field held on to the grain. Farmed paddy, wheat and maize now wait for people to thresh and sow them. People became part of the life cycle of these plants.
examples: The story goes that a Sufi saint named Baba Budan carried seven coffee beans from Yemen to the hills of Chikkamagaluru, around 1670.
Ragi, the finger millet of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, was first farmed in East Africa. Ragi probably reached India more than 3,000 years ago.
A maize cob is wrapped so tightly in leaves that the kernels have no way out unless someone opens the cob.
explanations.art: An old sailing ship on the sea between two coasts, with a line of small pictures above it going one way (chilli, tomato, potato, maize) and another line going the other way (pepper, mango, sugarcane).

explanations.definition: A crop is not one kind of plant. A crop is thousands of varieties, each a little different. Saving seeds means keeping those varieties alive, in fields or in seed banks.
explanations.description: For thousands of years every farmer saved seed from each harvest to sow the next year. In each valley the crop slowly changed to suit that soil and weather. India once had many thousands of rice varieties. Some stand in deep flood water. Some grow in salty soil near the sea. Some ripen in 60 days. In the last hundred years, most farmers moved to a few high-yield varieties, and many old ones were lost. Why does that matter? If every plant in a field is nearly the same, one disease can kill them all. In Ireland in the 1840s, most people grew one variety of potato. A disease called blight destroyed the crop year after year, and about a million people died. Variety is also where cures are found. In the 1970s a virus called grassy stunt was destroying rice across Asia. Scientists tested more than 6,000 kinds of rice from a seed bank. Only one could resist the virus. That one was a wild rice collected in Uttar Pradesh. Breeders crossed that wild rice with farmed rice, and made new varieties that resist the virus. There are two ways to save seeds. A seed bank keeps dry seeds in the cold, where they stay alive for decades. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway is inside a frozen mountain and holds more than a million samples. The other way is to keep sowing. Farmers such as Rahibai Popere in Maharashtra grow old varieties every year and share the seed. A variety that is sown every year keeps changing slowly. In each year, the plants that cope best with that year's weather and pests leave the most seed. Seeds in a vault stay as they were.
examples: Nikolai Vavilov, a Russian scientist, collected seeds on five continents and built the first great seed bank, in Leningrad.
At the yearly paddy festival started by Nel Jayaraman in Tamil Nadu, a farmer takes old rice seed home and brings back more the next year.
In Telangana, women of the Deccan Development Society keep village seed banks of millets and pulses in clay pots.
explanations.art: A woman sitting on a veranda among clay pots and cloth bundles of seeds, each with a label, holding out a handful of seeds to a child.

explanations.concept: Does a plant decide when to let a seed go?
explanations.description: A plant has some control over dispersal. Seeds do not all fall as soon as they are ripe. The stalk that holds a winged seed is strong enough to hold in a light breeze. It breaks in a strong, dry gust. So more seeds leave in exactly the kind of wind that carries them far. The scientist David Greene measured this on trees in 2005. A dandelion closes the tuft of hairs in damp air and opens it wide in dry air. In 2022, Madeleine Seale and her team showed how. A ring of tissue at the base of the hairs swells with water and pulls the hairs shut. Damp days usually have little wind, so the seeds stay at home on days when they would not go far. Plants sense, and they act on what they sense. Scientists agree about what happens. They do not agree about what to call it.
examples: A dandelion or tridax head is a wide ball on a dry afternoon and a closed brush on a wet morning.
Pine cones open their scales in dry weather and close them in wet weather.
Many trees with winged fruits hold them for weeks and lose most of them on a few windy days.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants sense and respond
perspectives.explanation: The plant senses dry air and strong wind, and lets the seeds go then. That is a decision. A decision does not need a brain. It needs sensing, and an action that depends on what was sensed.

The stalk snaps when the wind's pull is stronger than the stalk. The hairs close because wet tissue swells. These are simple physical events. They say the word 'decide' should be kept for animals with brains.
The timing was shaped over a very long time, because plants that let go in good winds left more young. Whether you call the result a decision depends on what you mean by the word.

explanations.art: The same dandelion seed head drawn twice: wide open under a sun with seeds leaving on the wind, and closed tight under a rain cloud.

agreed.text: A winged or tufted seed is carried by moving air. The wing or tuft slows the fall, and gives no forward push.
agreed.evidence: In still air, winged seeds and paper models of them fall straight down. In wind tunnels the sideways distance grows with the wind speed and with the time of the fall.

agreed.text: A spinning winged seed gets extra lift from a whirl of air on the front edge of the wing.
agreed.evidence: David Lentink's team saw this whirl on model maple seeds in a tank of oil in 2009. They then found the same whirl around real spinning seeds in a wind tunnel.

agreed.text: Most seeds land close to the parent plant, and a few travel very far.
agreed.evidence: Scientists set out trays to catch seeds at different distances from trees. The trays near the tree catch the most by far. Plants also reach new islands and bare ground, which only far-travelling seeds could do.

agreed.text: Many seeds survive being eaten, and sprout after passing through an animal.
agreed.evidence: Seeds picked out of the droppings of birds, bats, civets and elephants sprout when they are sown. Charles Darwin grew plants from seeds that he took from bird droppings.

agreed.text: Chilli, tomato, potato, maize and groundnut came to India from the Americas within the last 500 years.
agreed.evidence: The wild relatives of these crops grow only in the Americas. Indian writings from before 1500 do not mention them. Old remains of these crops from before that time are found only in the Americas.

agreed.text: A crop with many varieties is safer from disease than a crop with one.
agreed.evidence: The potato blight of the 1840s in Ireland destroyed a crop that was nearly all one variety. In the 1970s, one wild rice from Uttar Pradesh gave the resistance that saved rice crops across Asia from grassy stunt virus.

challenging.claim: Winged seeds fly, in the way that birds do.
challenging.who: A common way of speaking, found in many children's books.
challenging.for: Winged seeds do travel through the air, and some go a long way.
challenging.against: A bird pushes air backwards and down with muscles, and so moves forward. A seed has nothing to push with. In still air a winged seed only comes down slowly. The wind does all the sideways carrying.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a winged seed flies or is carried.

challenging.claim: Chilli, tomato and potato have always been part of Indian food.
challenging.who: A common belief, because these foods are in almost every Indian kitchen today.
challenging.for: They have been grown in India for many generations, and many Indian varieties exist nowhere else.
challenging.against: All three came from the Americas after 1498. Before that, Indian cooks used black pepper, long pepper, ginger and mustard for heat. A food can be truly part of a place and still have come from somewhere else.
challenging.context: This card is about where some of India's best-known foods first grew.

challenging.claim: Seeds are safest in a frozen seed bank.
challenging.for: Dry seeds kept at 18 degrees below zero stay alive for decades. A seed bank can hold a million samples in one building, safe from drought and war. Seeds from the Svalbard vault were used to rebuild a collection that was lost in the war in Syria.
challenging.against: Farmers and scientists such as Debal Deb say that frozen seeds stop changing, while the weather, pests and diseases outside keep changing. They also say that the knowledge of how to grow and cook each variety lives with farmers, and is not stored in a vault. Most people who work with seeds now say that both ways are needed.
challenging.context: This card is about the best way to keep old crop varieties alive: in a cold seed bank, or in farmers' fields.

challenging.claim: People should move trees to cooler places, because the climate is warming faster than seeds can travel.
challenging.who: Some forest scientists. They call this assisted migration.
challenging.for: Many trees disperse seeds only a short way in each generation, and a tree takes many years to make seeds. The places where they can live are moving faster than that.
challenging.against: People have moved plants with good intentions before, and some became invasive species. Lantana was brought to India as a garden flower. A moved plant can behave in unexpected ways in a new place.
challenging.context: This card is about whether people should carry the seeds of wild trees to new places on purpose.

challenging.claim: Some large fruits were shaped for giant animals who are now gone.
challenging.who: Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin, in 1982.
challenging.for: Some trees in the Americas make large, tough fruits that no wild animal living there now can swallow. The fruits rot under the tree. Giant ground sloths and elephant-like animals lived there until about 12,000 years ago.
challenging.against: It is very hard to test what an animal who no longer lives used to eat. Some of these trees are also dispersed by water, by rodents or by people. Many scientists accept the idea for a few trees and doubt it for others.
challenging.context: This card is about fruits that seem too large for any animal now living near them.

big_questions.q: A winged seed has no say in where the wind goes. Is the seed travelling, or being moved?
big_questions.hint: Think about a person on a bus, and a leaf in a river. What is the difference, if any?

big_questions.q: A mother tree makes ten thousand seeds and perhaps one becomes a tree. Were the others wasted?
big_questions.hint: Think about who ate them, and what would happen if the tree made only one seed.

big_questions.q: Farmed paddy needs people to sow the seed. People need paddy to eat. Who domesticated whom?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many paddy plants there were before farming, and how many there are now.

big_questions.q: The chilli came to India 500 years ago. Is the chilli an Indian plant now? How long does a plant need to belong?
big_questions.hint: Think about tamarind, which came thousands of years ago, and lantana, which came 200 years ago.

big_questions.q: A company can own a new variety of seed. Farmers bred the old varieties over thousands of years. Who should own seeds?
big_questions.hint: Think about who did the work, who needs the seed, and what happens if only a few people own all of it.

big_questions.q: A seed vault keeps seeds for a future nobody can see. What else should people keep safe for those who are not born yet?
big_questions.hint: Think about languages, forests, songs and clean water.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that seeds can cross a sea by themselves? This card tells the true story of Charles Darwin and his jars of salt water.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1850s, botanists had a puzzle. The same kinds of plants grew on islands and on mainlands hundreds of kilometres apart. Most botanists were sure that sea water kills seeds. So Edward Forbes and others said that land must once have joined those places, and had since sunk under the sea. Charles Darwin doubted it. Nobody had tested the seeds. In 1855, at his home in England, he filled jars with salt water and put in seeds of 87 kinds of plants. After 28 days he sowed them. Seeds of 64 kinds sprouted. A few kinds still sprouted after 137 days. Then Darwin found a problem. Most fresh seeds sink within days. So he tried dried branches with ripe fruits on them, as a flood might carry. Many floated for weeks. He looked up the speed of Atlantic currents and worked out that seeds could drift about 1,500 kilometres. He also grew 537 seedlings from three spoonfuls of pond mud, of the kind that sticks to a duck's feet. No sunken land was needed.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Darwin, an English naturalist (1809 to 1882), with questions and doubts from his friend the botanist Joseph Hooker
how_we_found_out.when: Darwin did the salt water tests in 1855 and 1856. He described them in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That sea water quickly kills seeds, so plants could only reach islands across land that has since sunk. Darwin showed that the seeds of most kinds he tested were still alive after four weeks in salt water, and that dried fruits can float for weeks.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1850s clothes in a study, bending over a row of glass jars of water with seeds in them, with pots of small seedlings on the windowsill.

roots.context: In this unit you tested paper fliers in the wind of a fan, and followed seeds across seas and kitchens. Here we ask what those journeys show about plants, about the world and about us.

deep_truth.truth: In the Fan Lane Test, the packed strip and the spinner were the same paper with the same clip. The fan blew equally on both. The spinner landed far away, because the wings gave the moving air more to push on and more time to push. So a winged seed does not fly. The wing only slows the fall, and the wind does all the carrying.
deep_truth.habit: We say that seeds fly and that plants spread, as if they went by their own power. We think that to travel, a being must move themself. A plant travels by being ready for something else that is already moving.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Fan Lane Test, the design that took longest to fall in still air also landed farthest in the wind. With the fan off, every design landed at your feet. Nothing in the paper pushed forward.

three.who_am_i: Your body was built from food. Much of that food came from plants whose seeds crossed oceans in ships and pockets. You are partly made of long journeys that other people and other beings made.
three.what_is_life: A plant stays in one spot for a whole life. But each seed is a chance to live somewhere else. So a kind of plant keeps moving across the land, one generation at a time.
three.what_is_this_world: Wind, rivers, sea currents, birds, bats, ants, elephants and people all carry seeds. The map of where each plant lives was drawn by everything that moves.

roots.thread: A tree is one being, rooted in one place. From that one tree come thousands of seeds, and they go out in every direction. The tree does not do the moving. The Sun warms the air and makes the wind, the rain fills the river, and a bird is hungry. Each of them takes a seed somewhere new. So the one tree becomes many trees only with the help of the whole world around them. And the forest that grows up feeds the birds and holds the rain in return.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to bring a fruit of the banyan and break it open. Inside are tiny seeds. He asks him to break one seed, and the boy says he sees nothing inside. Uddalaka says that the great banyan tree grows from that fine essence which he cannot see.
teachings.link: A banyan seed is smaller than a mustard seed, small enough to pass through a bird and be dropped on a far wall. The teaching and the science both look at how something so small can hold a whole tree. The Upanishad is speaking about the self and the world, not about botany.
verse: किमत्र पश्यसीति । न किंचन भगव इति
तं होवाच यं वै सोम्यैतमणिमानं न निभालयस एतस्य वै सोम्यैषोऽणिम्न एवं महान्यग्रोधस्तिष्ठति

teachings.source: The Gospel of Matthew 13:3-8, the parable of the sower
teachings.teaching: A sower scatters seed. Some falls on the path, and birds eat that seed. Some falls on rock and withers. Some falls among thorns and is choked. Some falls on good soil and gives a large harvest.
teachings.link: This is a seed shadow, told two thousand years ago. Most seeds land in the wrong place, and the few that land well make up for all the rest. The parable is about people who hear a teaching, but the picture of the seeds is exact.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988), on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Thich Nhat Hanh, a Vietnamese Buddhist teacher, wrote that if you look deeply at a sheet of paper you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud there is no rain, without rain no tree, and without the tree no paper.
teachings.link: Look at a chilli in the same way. In the chilli there is a bird who carried the seed, a ship that crossed an ocean, and a farmer who saved the seed each year for 500 years.

science.text: A wind-dispersed seed has no source of forward push. The distance travelled comes from the wind speed, the release height and the fall speed.
Many plants let seeds go mostly in dry, gusty weather, when seeds travel farthest. Whether this should be called a decision is argued about.
Farmed rice, wheat and maize have lost the ability to scatter their own seeds, and depend on people to sow them.

other_view.who: Many plant scientists, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: On this view, a seed on the wind is matter moved by matter. The wing is a shape that happened to leave more young, and was passed on. Dry air and a strong gust are enough to explain when a seed lets go. They would say that words such as 'ready' and 'help' are ours, and that we put them into the story.

practice.title: Let go and watch
practice.say: Stand up and hold your paper spinner as high as you can. Take one slow breath in. As you breathe out, open your fingers. Do not throw and do not push. Watch the spinner all the way to the floor. Notice that you did nothing after letting go. Do this three times. Then sit down, and breathe in and out slowly three times. Feel the air move in and out. That is the same air that carried the spinner.
practice.kid: Hold your spinner up high. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out and open your fingers. Do not push. Watch the spinner fall all the way. Do it three times. Then sit and breathe slowly three times.

ask: A seed goes where the wind goes. When have you been carried somewhere good by something you did not plan?
The tomato in your sambar had ancestors in South America. Where does a food come from: where it grows now, or where it began?
A tree lets go of ten thousand seeds and never finds out which one lived. Could you make something and let it go like that?
roots.art: A child standing with one arm raised high and fingers just opened, watching a paper spinner turn in the air above the floor.

story.title: The Black Rock
story.note: Tunga, Kiran, Doddamma and their village are made up, and so is the fire. These things are real. The honne tree, also called Indian kino or vengai, grows in the forests of Uttara Kannada in Karnataka. Each pod is flat and round, about as wide as a biscuit, with one seed in the middle and a papery wing all round. The pods ripen in the dry season and are carried by the wind. Hill slopes in these forests do burn in the dry months, and wind-carried seeds are among the first to arrive on burnt ground. Doddamma means a mother's elder sister in Kannada.
text: The fire came in February, on the far side of the stream. It took one night to climb the hill from the water to the ridge. In the morning the slope across from Tunga's house was black. By March it was the colour of a brick, with nothing on it but stones.
"It will be green again," said Doddamma. She was Tunga's mother's elder sister, and she had walked that forest as a watcher for nineteen years. "Grass in two years. Trees later."
"How much later?"
"After my time, perhaps." She said it without any sadness, and went on shelling beans.

Tunga did not want to wait until after anyone's time. On their own side of the stream stood the honne, the tallest tree in the village, older than the house. In March the pods were ripe. Each one was flat and brown and no bigger than a biscuit, with a hard bump in the middle where the seed lay, and a papery frill all the way round.
She filled a basket with them. Then she took her cousin Kiran, who was seven and came whether he was asked or not, and went down to the bank.
Nobody could cross. The stream ran in a deep cut there, and Doddamma had forbidden the burnt hill in any case. The ground was loose, she said, and a slope with no roots in it slides.
So Tunga threw. She threw the first pod as hard as she could. It went up, turned on its edge, and fluttered down three steps from her feet.
Kiran laughed and threw one like a cricket ball. His came down two steps away.
They threw until their shoulders ached. The bank around them was brown with pods, and not one had reached the water.
"They are too light," said Kiran. "Make them heavy." He pressed five pods into a lump of wet clay from the bank and threw that. It sailed over the stream and hit the red slope with a smack.
They made twenty clay balls before dark, and nineteen of them crossed.

The next morning Tunga looked at the hill for a long time. She could see every ball, because each had left a pale mark. The marks made one crooked line along the very bottom of the slope, just above the water. That was as far as a boy's arm could send a lump of clay. Above the line, the hill went up and up, higher than ten temple towers, and there was nothing on it at all.
In the afternoon she sat under the honne with the empty basket and was cross with everything.
The wind came up the valley, as it did every afternoon in March, hot and steady from behind her. High in the tree, something let go.

She watched it because there was nothing else to watch. It was a pod from the topmost branch, and it did not drop. It turned over and over, slowly, and as it turned it slid away sideways on the wind. It was still in the air when it passed over the cowshed. It came down in the lane.
Tunga got up and walked from the trunk to the lane, counting. Forty-one steps.
Then she walked back and looked under the tree. Around the roots, the pods from the low branches lay in a heap, one on top of another.
The same pods. The same wind. She looked up at the top branch, and then at the lowest one, which she could nearly touch.
The tree had not thrown anything. The tree had only let go, from high up, when the wind was blowing. And the pod had taken a long time to come down.

That was the whole of it, she thought. A long time. A pod she threw was on the ground again in one breath. The pod from the top had stayed up while she could have counted to twelve, and the wind had been carrying it for all twelve.

Above the house the goat path climbed to the Black Rock, a ledge that stuck out over the valley. It was three times as high as the honne. From there the burnt hill lay across from you and a little below.

The next day she carried a full basket up, with Kiran behind her complaining about his legs. They reached the ledge at noon. The air was dead still. She held one pod out and let it go, and it tumbled straight down onto the rocks under their feet.
"See?" said Kiran. "You have to throw it."
"No. We have to wait."
They ate their rotti. They watched a kite circle. A little after three, the dry grass at the edge of the ledge began to lean.
Tunga laid one pod flat on her open palm and lifted her hand above her head. She did nothing else. The wind took the pod off her hand.
It went out over the stream, turning. It kept going. It grew small, and then smaller, a brown fleck against the red, and she lost sight of it before it ever came down.
For once Kiran said nothing. Then he said, "Give me some."
"Don't throw."
"I know," he said, and opened his hand.
They let the whole basket go, a few pods at a time, whenever the grass leaned. Some dropped into the stream. Some swung round and landed in their own trees. Most of them they could not follow at all.
Doddamma heard about it at supper. "Most will be eaten," she said. "Beetles. Mice. Most of the rest will dry up on the stones."
"I know."
"Then why carry them all that way?"
"The tree does the same," said Tunga.
Doddamma looked out at the honne for a while. Then she went back to her plate.
The rains came in June. By August the far hill had a green haze on it, and from the ledge Tunga could not tell what was grass and what was not.

The next March, Doddamma crossed the stream lower down, on her rounds, and climbed the burnt hill with a stick. She came home at dusk and put a leaf on the table. It was a small leaf made of several leaflets, and each leaflet had a tiny notch at the tip.
"Honne," she said. "High up, near the ridge. No ball of clay ever got there."
"How many?"
"I found four. I did not look everywhere." She sat down. "They may be yours. They may be the old tree's own. The wind does not sign its work."

Tunga tried to remember how many pods the basket had held. Hundreds. She pressed the leaf between two pages of her science notebook. Then she went outside to see whether the grass had started to lean.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Tunga tries to get seeds across the stream by throwing harder, and then by making them heavier. Both fail, because strength and weight are the wrong things to change. A honne pod travels because the papery wing makes the fall slow, and the wind carries the pod for as long as the fall lasts. So what matters is how high the pod starts and whether the wind is blowing. The clay balls crossed the stream, but they fell fast, so they reached only the bottom of the hill. The pods released from the high ledge in the afternoon wind reached the top. The story never says the words drag or fall speed. Let your child find the idea in the pod from the top branch.
ask: Tunga threw a pod as hard as she could and it landed three steps away. Why did throwing hard not help?
The clay balls crossed the stream. Why was Tunga still not happy with them?
The pod from the top branch landed forty-one steps away, and the pods from the low branches lay in a heap. What made the difference?
On the ledge at noon, the pod fell straight down. What were they waiting for, and why?
Doddamma said that most of the seeds would be eaten or dry up. Was it still worth doing? What would you have done?

games.title: Seed Drift: nuts and winged seeds on a windy hill
games.context: This is a dice game about where seeds land. You are a tree on a hill. You let go six seeds, and the die is the wind. A winged seed stays in the air for six rolls and a heavy nut for only two.

printables.title: The hillside board: draw a row of 21 squares on a long strip of paper and number them 0 to 20
items: Square 0: draw the mother tree here
Squares 0, 1 and 2: UNDER THE MOTHER TREE. Shade them grey. A nut scores 1 point here. A winged seed scores 0
Squares 3 to 8: OPEN GROUND. Colour them green. Any seed scores 2 points here
Squares 9, 10 and 11: THE STREAM. Colour them blue. Any seed scores 0 here
Squares 12 to 20: THE BARE HILL. Colour them red-brown. Any seed scores 5 points here

printables.title: What the die means: copy these lines beside the board
items: 1 or 2: CALM. The seed does not move
3 or 4: BREEZE. Move the seed 1 square
A nut is in the air for 2 rolls. A winged seed is in the air for 6 rolls

rules: You need the hillside board, one die, a pencil, and 6 seeds for each player. Use chana for nuts and moong for winged seeds.
Before you start, choose your 6 seeds. You may take any mix, such as 3 chana and 3 moong, or 6 of one kind.
On your turn, put one seed on square 0. That seed has just left the mother tree.
For a nut, roll the die 2 times. For a winged seed, roll the die 6 times. After each roll, move the seed as the die says.
After the last roll, the seed lands. Leave the seed on that square and write down the points for that square.
A seed that would pass square 20 stops on square 20.
Then the next player takes a turn. Play until every seed has landed.
The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Play all 6 seeds and add up your points. A score of 10 or more is a good game. Play again with a different mix and compare.

setup.art: A long strip of paper with 21 numbered squares, a small tree drawn at square 0, and bands of grey, green, blue and red-brown.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board: 21 squares, from the mother tree to the bare hill.

setup.art: A hand holding three chana and three moong seeds over the board, beside a die.
setup.caption: 2. Choose 6 seeds. Chana are nuts and moong are winged seeds.

setup.art: A moong seed on square 7 of the board with a die showing 5 beside it, and a pencil tally of rolls.
setup.caption: 3. Roll for the wind. A nut gets 2 rolls and a winged seed gets 6.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board and copy what the die means. 2. Each player chooses a mix of 6 seeds. 3. Ask why each player chose that mix.
flow.say: This board is a hillside. Your tree stands on square 0. Which seeds will you make, nuts or winged seeds? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Choose 6 seeds. Chana are nuts. Moong are winged seeds. Say why you chose your mix.

ask.q: Why does a winged seed get 6 rolls and a nut only 2?
good: The winged seed falls slowly, so the wind has more time to move the seed.
The nut is heavy for its size and reaches the ground quickly.

flow.parent: The number of rolls stands for the time in the air. This is the main idea of the unit: the wind can only carry a seed while the seed is still falling.
flow.context: This is the first step of Seed Drift. You draw the hillside board and choose your six seeds.

flow.do: Play until each player has landed 3 seeds. Then stop and ask the question below.
flow.say: Roll for the wind and move your seed. Watch where the nuts land and where the winged seeds land.
flow.kid: Roll the die. Move your seed. A nut gets 2 rolls. A winged seed gets 6. Write your points.

ask.q: Has any nut reached the bare hill? Could one ever get there?
good: No. A nut can move 6 squares at most, with two gusts.
The bare hill starts at square 12, so a nut can never reach it.

flow.parent: A nut can travel at most 6 squares. Only a winged seed can cross the stream. But a winged seed can also land in the stream, and scores nothing under the mother tree.
flow.context: In this step of Seed Drift you play the first half of the game.

flow.do: 1. Play until every seed has landed. 2. Add up the points. 3. Look at where all the seeds lie on the board. 4. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Finish the game and add up. Now look at the whole board. Where did most of the seeds land? Did any go very far?
flow.kid: Finish the game. Add up your points. Look at the board. Where did most seeds land?

ask.q: Which did better in your game, the nuts or the winged seeds? Would that be the same on every hill?
good: The winged seeds, because one reached the bare hill.
The nuts, because the winged seeds fell in the stream.
It depends on what the ground is like near the tree and far away.

check.q: In Seed Drift, a winged seed and a nut leave the same tree in the same wind. Why does the winged seed usually land farther away?
options: The winged seed stays in the air longer
The winged seed pushes forward with the wing
The wind blows harder on small seeds
check.why: The wind moves a seed only while the seed is in the air. A winged seed falls slowly, so the wind has more time. Choosing 'pushes forward' means thinking of a wing as an engine. A seed's wing has no power.

flow.think: A real tree makes thousands of seeds, not six. How would the board look with a thousand seeds on it?
flow.context: This is the last step of Seed Drift. You finish the game and look at the pattern of landed seeds.

games.title: Who Carried Me? Three clues, three points
games.context: This is a clue game about how seeds travel. Each card gives three clues about a fruit or a seed, from hard to easy. You say who or what carries the seed. The sooner you get it, the more points you score.

printables.title: 16 clue cards: three clues on the front, the answer on the back

items.f: Clue 1: My skin keeps water out. Clue 2: Under the skin is a thick coat of fibres with air between them. Clue 3: I can float for a hundred days.
items.b: THE SEA. I am a coconut.

items.f: Clue 1: I am one of hundreds on a small white ball by the roadside. Clue 2: I am as thin as a pencil line. Clue 3: I wear a ring of feathery hairs on top.
items.b: THE WIND. I am a tridax fruit, with a parachute of hairs.

items.f: Clue 1: I grew on a tall roadside tree, inside a woody case as big as a fist. Clue 2: I have one long wing. Clue 3: I spin like a helicopter blade as I fall.
items.b: THE WIND. I am a mahogany seed.

items.f: Clue 1: I grew in a long pod that hung like a stick. Clue 2: People cook the young pod in sambar. Clue 3: I have three papery wings.
items.b: THE WIND. I am a drumstick seed.

items.f: Clue 1: I sprouted while I was still hanging on my mother. Clue 2: I am long and green, like a fat pencil. Clue 3: I drop into salty mud or float away on the tide.
items.b: THE SEA. I am a mangrove seedling.

items.f: Clue 1: I am smaller than a mustard seed. Clue 2: I sat inside a small red fig. Clue 3: I often sprout high on a wall or on another tree.
items.b: BIRDS AND BATS. They ate the fig and dropped me. I am a banyan or peepal seed.

items.f: Clue 1: My fruit turns red when I am ready. Clue 2: Rats and mice hate the taste. Clue 3: Birds do not sense the burning at all.
items.b: BIRDS. I am a chilli seed.

items.f: Clue 1: I grew on a grass in a field or a park. Clue 2: I have a sharp point. Clue 3: You pull me out of your socks.
items.b: FUR, FEATHERS AND CLOTHES. I am a spear grass seed, and I cling.

items.f: Clue 1: My pod is fat, green and under strain. Clue 2: The walls of my pod want to curl. Clue 3: One touch, and they fling me out.
items.b: MY OWN PLANT. I am a balsam seed, and the pod throws me.

items.f: Clue 1: My dry case snaps open in the sun and throws me. Clue 2: I carry a small oily bump. Clue 3: Ants carry me home for that bump.
items.b: MY OWN PLANT, AND THEN ANTS. I am a castor seed.

items.f: Clue 1: My wild cousins drop their grain into the water. Clue 2: I hold on tight to my stalk. Clue 3: I wait to be threshed and sown.
items.b: PEOPLE. I am a grain of farmed paddy.

items.f: Clue 1: I am large, flat and hairy, inside sweet yellow flesh. Clue 2: Elephants, monkeys and bats carry my fruit. Clue 3: People spit me out in summer.
items.b: LARGE ANIMALS, AND PEOPLE. I am a mango seed.

items.f: Clue 1: People brought my grandparents to India for their pretty flowers. Clue 2: My berries are small and dark. Clue 3: Bulbuls eat them, and now I cover whole forests.
items.b: PEOPLE FIRST, THEN BIRDS. I am a lantana seed.

items.f: Clue 1: A million of us fit in one pod. Clue 2: I have no food store at all. Clue 3: I am as fine as dust.
items.b: THE WIND. I am an orchid seed.

items.f: Clue 1: My flower opened above the ground. Clue 2: Then a stalk pushed me down into the soil. Clue 3: I ripen under the earth, beside my parent.
items.b: NOBODY. I am a groundnut, and I stay at home unless a person or an animal digs me up.

items.f: Clue 1: My pod is fat and green on a grey bush by the road. Clue 2: The pod splits when ripe. Clue 3: I am flat and brown, with long silky hairs.
items.b: THE WIND. I am a calotropis seed, also called erukku or aak.

rules: You need the 16 clue cards, and paper and a pencil for the scores.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clues facing down.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads clue 1 only.
The guesser says who or what carries this seed. A right answer after clue 1 scores 3 points.
If the guess is wrong, or the guesser asks to wait, the reader reads clue 2. A right answer now scores 2 points.
After clue 3, a right answer scores 1 point.
A guesser who also names the plant gets 1 extra point.
Swap the reader after every card. The game ends when the pile is finished. The most points wins.
Playing alone? Cover clues 2 and 3 with your hand and read one clue at a time. A score of 30 or more out of 64 is very good.

setup.art: A pile of small paper cards face down, and one card held up showing three numbered clues.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. Put them in a pile, clues down.

setup.art: A girl reading from a card while a younger boy thinks with his chin on his hand.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads clue 1. Who or what carries this seed?

setup.art: A score sheet with two names and tally marks, beside a card turned over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Score 3, 2 or 1 points, and 1 extra for naming the plant.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Read the rules together. 3. Play one card as practice, with no score.
flow.say: Each card is a seed speaking. The first clue is the hardest. Listen for the shape, the weight and the covering.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the rules. Try one card for practice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Carried Me? You make the cards and try one.

flow.do: Play the first 8 cards. Write each player's points. After card 8, ask the question below.
flow.say: Listen to the first clue. What could carry a seed like that? Guess now, or wait for the next clue.
flow.kid: Listen to clue 1. Guess if you are sure. Wait for the next clue if you are not.

ask.q: Which clues told you 'wind' straight away? What do those seeds share?
good: Wings or hairs.
They are very light.
They have a wide surface for their weight.

flow.parent: Ask for the evidence each time: which word in the clue made you say that? The shape is evidence, not proof.
flow.context: In this step of Who Carried Me? you play the first eight cards.

flow.do: 1. Play the last 8 cards. 2. Add up the points. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Finish the pile and add up. Which card surprised you most?
flow.kid: Play the last 8 cards. Add up your points. Which card surprised you?

check.q: A fruit is soft, sweet and bright red, with small hard seeds inside. Who most likely carries the seeds?
options: An animal who eats the fruit
The wind
The sea
check.why: Sweet flesh and a bright colour are a payment and a signal for an animal. The hard seeds pass through the animal whole. Choosing 'the wind' misses that a juicy fruit is far too heavy for wind and has no wing.

ask.q: The groundnut card said 'nobody'. Why might staying beside the parent work for some plants?
good: The parent grew well there, so the place is good.
The seeds are hidden from seed-eaters under the soil.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Carried Me? You finish the cards and add up.

experiments.title: The Fan Lane Test: same paper, same weight, three shapes. Which travels farthest in the same wind?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three paper fliers from strips of the same size, each with one paper clip. One is packed tight, one has short wings and one has long wings. You time how long each takes to fall in still air. Then you let each go in front of a fan and measure how far away they land.
experiments.question: Three fliers weigh the same and meet the same wind. Does the shape change how far they travel? Does the one that falls slowest also travel farthest?
experiments.predict: Guess before any drop. Which flier will take longest to fall in still air? Which will land farthest from the fan, and about how far? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All three fliers are cut from the same sheet, to the same size, and each carries one paper clip of the same size. So they weigh the same, and only the shape differs. Each one is let go from the same spot, with no push, in the same wind. You repeat every drop, because moving air is never perfectly steady. A fan's wind is narrow and gets weaker farther away. So this is a model of a windy day, and not a copy of one.
results_table: Fall time in still air: tries 1, 2 and 3 (seconds)
Distance in the fan lane: tries 1 to 5 (cm)

materials.item: sheet of A4 paper, or a page from a long notebook
paper clips of the same size
scissors, a ruler and a pencil
table fan or pedestal fan. If you have neither, use an air cooler, or a hair dryer on the cool setting held steady on a pile of books by a grown-up
measuring tape, or a ruler and a long piece of string
phone with a stopwatch
small pieces of tape or chalk, to mark the floor
clear floor at least 3 metres long, in a room with the windows shut and the ceiling fan off

experiments.safety: Keep fingers, hair and paper away from the fan blades. A grown-up holds the fliers up for the 2-metre drops. Nobody stands on a chair alone.
experiments.record: Fill in one row of the table for each flier. Work out the mean fall time and the mean distance. Draw a bar chart of the three mean distances. Then write three sentences: what I thought would happen, what I saw, and why I think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean distance from the start mark in the fan lane
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your own numbers will differ, because fans, paper and paper clips differ.

setup.art: Three strips of paper on a table: one with two long wings folded opposite ways and a paper clip on a narrow stem, one the same with the wings folded back to half length, and one folded into a small packet held by a clip.
setup.caption: 1. Make three fliers from strips of the same size: long wings, short wings and packed.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a paper spinner up beside a pencil mark on a door frame 2 metres above the floor, with a child below holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. With all fans off, time each flier falling from 2 metres. Do it three times each.

setup.art: A table fan on a table blowing along a clear floor, a child's hand holding a paper spinner 50 centimetres in front of the fan, and a tape mark on the floor below the hand.
setup.caption: 3. Switch on the fan. Let each flier go from the same spot, with no push.

setup.art: A child measuring with a tape along the floor from a tape mark near the fan to a paper spinner lying two steps away.
setup.caption: 4. Measure from the start mark to where each flier landed. Do it five times each.

flow.do: 1. Cut three strips from one sheet. Each strip is 21 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. 2. Long wings: cut a slit 9 centimetres long down the middle of one end. Just below the slit, cut in 1.5 centimetres from each side. Fold the two sides of the lower part in, to make a narrow stem. Fold the end of the stem up by 2 centimetres and slide a paper clip on. Fold one wing towards you and one away. 3. Short wings: make a second spinner in the same way. Then fold each wing back on itself, so each wing is half as long. Press the folds hard. 4. Packed: fold the third strip in half three times. Hold the packet shut with a paper clip.
flow.say: We are making three paper models of seeds. Each has the same paper and the same clip. What is the same about them? What is different?
flow.kid: Cut three strips of the same size. Make one spinner with long wings. Make one with short wings. Fold the third strip into a small packet. Put one clip on each.

ask.q: All three have the same paper and the same clip. So what can we say about their weight?
good: They weigh the same.
Only the shape is different.

flow.parent: The paper clip stands for the seed, and the paper for the fruit round the seed. Check that the two wings of each spinner are folded opposite ways, like a letter T seen from the side.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fan Lane Test. You make three paper fliers that weigh the same and differ only in shape.

flow.do: 1. Put the three fliers in a row. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Write down each guess and each reason. Do not say who is right.
flow.say: Which one will take longest to fall? Which will land farthest from the fan? About how far? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at your three fliers. Which will fall slowest? Which will land farthest from the fan? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Will the fan push harder on one of them? Why?
good: Yes, on the long wings, because they are wider.
No, the fan blows the same on all of them.
The heavy-looking packet will not be moved much.

flow.parent: Many children say the packed strip is heavier. It is not. Do not correct this now. The question at the end comes back to it.
flow.context: In this step of the Fan Lane Test you guess which flier will fall slowest and which will travel farthest.

flow.do: 1. Switch off every fan and shut the windows. 2. Mark a height of 2 metres on a door frame. 3. A grown-up holds each flier at the mark and lets go. 4. Your child starts the stopwatch at the letting go and stops it at the landing. 5. Do three drops for each flier and write every time.
flow.say: First we test in still air. I will let go at 2 metres. Start the stopwatch when I let go. Stop it when the flier lands.
flow.kid: All fans are off. A grown-up drops each flier from 2 metres. You time the fall. Do three drops for each. Write every time.

ask.q: Where did each flier land in still air: under the hand, or somewhere else?
good: Right under the hand.
Very close to the wall. None of them went sideways.

flow.parent: The packed strip falls in about 0.6 seconds, which is hard to time by hand. A hand-timed fall can easily be 0.2 seconds out. That is why you take three tries. The long wings usually take 1.5 to 2 seconds. If a spinner flutters and does not spin, check the wing folds. If neither spinner spins, add a second clip to all three fliers.
flow.context: In this step of the Fan Lane Test you time each flier falling 2 metres in still air.

flow.do: 1. Put the fan on a table at one end of the clear floor. Set it to full speed. Stop it turning from side to side. 2. Hold a hand 50 centimetres in front of the fan, level with the middle of the fan. Put a tape mark on the floor right under your hand. This is the start mark. 3. Let each flier go from that spot, 5 times each. Do not push. 4. A helper watches where the flier first touches the floor, and marks the spot. 5. Measure from the start mark to each landing spot.
flow.say: Now the wind. Hold the flier in front of the fan and just open your fingers. I will mark where it first touches the floor.
flow.kid: Switch on the fan. Hold a flier in the wind. Open your fingers. Do not push. Mark where the flier lands. Measure from the start mark. Do 5 drops for each.

ask.q: The landing spots of one flier are not all the same. Why not?
good: The wind is not perfectly steady.
I may have let go a little differently each time.

check.q: In the Fan Lane Test, why is every flier let go from the same spot, with no push?
options: So that only the shape differs
So that the fan stays cool
So that the fliers spin faster
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. Here that one thing is the shape. If one flier got a push or a better spot, you could not tell what caused the difference. Choosing another answer means the idea of a fair test needs another look.

flow.parent: In the fan's wind a spinner may tumble at first and spin only later. Count every drop anyway. The packed strip usually lands within about 50 centimetres. The long wings often land 1 to 2 metres away, and sometimes more. Measure to where the flier first touched down, not to where the flier slid to.
flow.context: In this step of the Fan Lane Test you let each flier go in the wind of a fan and measure how far away they land.

flow.do: 1. For each flier, add the three fall times and divide by 3. 2. Add the five distances and divide by 5. 3. Write the fliers in order of fall time. Write them in order of distance. 4. Draw a bar for each mean distance.
flow.say: Work out the mean fall time and the mean distance for each flier. Put them in order both ways. Are the two orders the same?
flow.kid: Find the mean fall time for each flier. Find the mean distance. Put the fliers in order of time. Put them in order of distance. Are the orders the same?
flow.parent: A worked example: distances of 150, 190, 160, 210 and 140 centimetres add up to 850. Then 850 ÷ 5 = 170 centimetres. A calculator is fine.
flow.context: In this step of the Fan Lane Test you work out the means and compare fall time with distance.

flow.do: 1. Switch the fan off. Drop the long-wing spinner once more from the same spot, and see where it lands. 2. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 3. Only then read the note below together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Then say why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Switch the fan off. Drop the long wings again. Where do they land now? Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: All three weigh the same, and the fan blew the same on all three. So why did they land in different places?
good: The wings give the air more to push on.
The long wings fell slowly, so the wind had longer to carry them.
The packed strip fell before the wind could move it far.

ask.q: With the fan off, the long wings landed at the start mark. So what do the wings do, and what does the wind do?
good: The wings slow the fall.
The wind does the carrying.

flow.parent: Most families find that the flier with the longest fall time also travels farthest. Write down what you really found, even if it differs. The reason has two parts with one cause. A wing gives the air a wide surface to push on, for the same weight. So the fall is slow, and the wind has more time to carry the flier. The wind also brings a broad, light flier up to the wind's own speed quickly. The wing itself gives no forward push. With the fan off, every flier lands at your feet.
flow.think: A tree is ten times as tall as your drop. If the wind blew all the way down, about how much farther would a spinner from the treetop go?
