flow.context: This is the last step of the Fan Lane Test. You say what you found, and what a wing really does.

experiments.title: The Seed Shadow Test: where do 30 drops of the same spinner land?
experiments.context: In this experiment you let the same long-wing paper spinner go 30 times in front of a fan, from the same spot each time. You record how far away each drop lands, and draw the pattern. Scientists call the pattern of where a plant's seeds land a seed shadow.
experiments.question: When the same spinner is let go 30 times in the same wind, do all 30 land in the same place? If not, what is the shape of the pattern?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Will all 30 drops land in about the same place? Draw the pattern of 30 landing spots that you expect. Why do you think so? Write your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The same spinner is used for all 30 drops. The same person lets go, from the same spot, with no push. The fan stays at one speed and points one way. Nothing is changed on purpose, so any spread in the landings comes from the small changes in the moving air and in the letting go.

materials.item: long-wing paper spinner from the Fan Lane Test, or a new one made the same way
table fan or pedestal fan
measuring tape, or a ruler and string
pieces of tape, chalk or thread, to mark lines on the floor
notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Keep fingers, hair and paper away from the fan blades.
experiments.record: Make a tally for six bands: 0 to 50 centimetres, 50 to 100, 100 to 150, 150 to 200, 200 to 250, and beyond 250. Count the landings in each band. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each band. Write which band had the most landings, and how far the farthest drop went.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: where 30 drops of one spinner landed
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your own pattern will differ.

setup.art: A floor seen from above with a fan at one end, a tape mark in front of it, and five parallel lines of tape across the floor at equal gaps.
setup.caption: 1. From the start mark, put a line across the floor every 50 centimetres.

setup.art: A child letting a paper spinner go in front of a fan while a second child makes tally marks in a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Let the same spinner go 30 times. Tally the band where each drop lands.

setup.art: A child's bar chart on squared paper with six bars, the tallest in the middle and a very short bar at the far right.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each band. Look at the shape of the pattern.

flow.do: 1. Set up the fan and the start mark as in the Fan Lane Test. 2. Mark a line across the floor every 50 centimetres, up to 250 centimetres. 3. Ask for the prediction and the reason. Your child draws the pattern they expect.
flow.say: We will let the same spinner go 30 times. Nothing will change. Will all 30 land in the same place? Draw the pattern you expect. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark a line every 50 centimetres. You will drop one spinner 30 times. Will all the drops land together? Draw what you expect. Say why.

ask.q: If nothing is changed, why might the landings still differ?
good: The wind from a fan wobbles a little.
My fingers do not let go in exactly the same way.

flow.parent: Some children expect all 30 in one spot, because nothing is changed. Others expect an even spread. Do not correct either guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seed Shadow Test. You mark distance bands on the floor and predict the pattern of 30 landings.

flow.do: 1. Your child lets the spinner go from the start spot, with no push. 2. A helper calls out the band where the spinner first touches the floor. 3. Make one tally mark for that band. 4. Do this 30 times.
flow.say: Just open your fingers each time. I will call the band. You make the tally mark.
flow.kid: Let the spinner go. Do not push. See which band the spinner lands in. Make a tally mark. Do this 30 times.
flow.parent: If the spinner hits a wall or a chair, do that drop again. If the wings go soft, press the folds flat again. Thirty drops take about ten minutes.
flow.context: In this step of the Seed Shadow Test you let the spinner go 30 times and tally where each drop lands.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally marks in each band. 2. Draw a bar for each band. 3. Find the band with the most landings, and the farthest landing of all.
flow.say: Count each band and draw the bars. Which band has the most? How far did the farthest drop go?
flow.kid: Count your tally marks. Draw a bar for each band. Which band has the most? How far was the farthest drop?
flow.context: In this step of the Seed Shadow Test you draw a bar chart of the 30 landings.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they expected, what the chart shows, and why. 2. Then read the note below together. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Say what you expected. Say what the chart shows. Why do you think the drops did not all land together?
flow.kid: Say what you expected. Say what your chart shows. Say why the drops spread out.

ask.q: Suppose only the ground beyond 200 centimetres is good for growing. How many of your 30 seeds reached that ground?
good: Only two or three.
None this time, but one came close.

ask.q: A tree lets go ten thousand seeds, not thirty. What does that do to the number that go very far?
good: Many more of them will go very far.
Even a rare far trip will happen many times.

check.q: A tree's seed shadow is the pattern of where the tree's seeds land. What does a seed shadow usually look like?
options: Most seeds near, a few far
All seeds at one distance
The same number at every distance
check.why: Most seeds leave on an ordinary breeze and land near the parent. A few meet a strong gust or rising air and go far. Choosing 'all at one distance' means expecting the wind to be perfectly steady. Real wind never is.

flow.parent: Most families find the landings bunched in two or three bands, with a few drops well short or well beyond. A fan is much steadier than the wind outdoors, so the spread in a real seed shadow is far wider. To see this, do 30 more drops with the fan turning from side to side. Now the wind comes in gusts, and some drops get almost none.
flow.think: The farthest drop is rare. Why might that one seed matter more to the tree than the twenty that landed together?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Seed Shadow Test. You say what the pattern of landings shows.

experiments.title: Darwin's Jar: do seeds still sprout after a day and a night in sea water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you repeat a test that Charles Darwin did in 1855. You soak ten moong seeds in salt water as strong as the sea, and ten in plain water, for one day and one night. Then you rinse both lots, keep them damp, and count how many of each sprout.
experiments.question: Does a day and a night in sea water kill seeds? Which kitchen seeds and fruits could float across water at all?
experiments.predict: Guess before you start. Out of 10 moong seeds soaked in salt water, how many will sprout? Out of 10 soaked in plain water, how many? Why do you think so? Write both numbers and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Both lots of seeds come from the same packet. Both soak for the same time, and then sit on the same kind of damp cloth in the same place. Only one thing differs: salt in the soaking water. Ten seeds in each lot is a small number, so a difference of one or two seeds could be chance.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds from the kitchen
steel tumblers or glasses
drinking water, 1 tumbler for each lot
salt, 1 level teaspoon and a half for one tumbler of 200 millilitres
small pieces of clean cotton cloth, and two plates
for the float check: a groundnut in the shell, a whole dry red chilli, a cardamom pod, a few coriander seeds, a rajma bean and a piece of coir or coconut husk
two labels or slips of paper

experiments.safety: Nobody drinks the salt water. Throw away the seeds soaked in salt water at the end, and do not eat them.

schedule.what: Predict. Do the float check. Put 10 moong in salt water and 10 in plain water. Label both.
After about 24 hours, rinse both lots well. Put each lot on a damp cloth on a labelled plate.
Count the seeds with a root showing in each lot. Keep the cloths damp.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for both lots on day 3 and day 4. Write which things floated in plain water and which floated in salt water. Then write three sentences: what I thought would happen, what I saw, and why I think it happened.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers of water side by side with paper labels reading SALT and PLAIN, a teaspoon of salt, and a small heap of green moong seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Make salt water as strong as the sea in one tumbler. Leave the other plain.

setup.art: A tumbler of water with a groundnut in its shell, a dry red chilli and a cardamom pod floating on top and a rajma bean lying at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Float check: which kitchen seeds and fruits float, and which sink?

setup.art: Two plates, each with a damp white cloth and ten moong seeds on it, with labels SALT and PLAIN.
setup.caption: 3. After one day and one night, rinse both lots and put them on damp cloths.

setup.art: A child counting sprouted moong seeds with short white roots on a damp cloth and writing a number in a notebook.
setup.caption: 4. On days 3 and 4, count how many seeds in each lot have sprouted.

flow.do: 1. Stir one and a half level teaspoons of salt into one tumbler of water. Label it SALT. Label the other tumbler PLAIN. 2. Float check: drop the groundnut, chilli, cardamom, coriander, rajma and coir into the plain water. Write which float. Then try them in the salt water. 3. Take them out. Ask for the prediction. 4. Put 10 moong seeds in each tumbler.
flow.say: This salt water is about as salty as the sea. Which of these will float? Now the moong. How many of 10 will sprout after a day in sea water? Why?
flow.kid: Make salt water in one tumbler. Test which things float. Then put 10 moong in each tumbler. Guess how many will sprout. Say why.

ask.q: What do the floaters have that the sinkers do not?
good: Air inside.
A dry, light covering.
A shell with a gap between the shell and the seed.

flow.parent: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in each litre. A level teaspoon of salt is about 5 grams, so one and a half teaspoons in 200 millilitres is close. Groundnuts in the shell, dry chillies, cardamom pods, coriander and coir usually float. Rajma and moong sink. A thing that only just sinks in plain water may float in salt water, because salt water is denser.
flow.wait: Leave both tumblers for about 24 hours
flow.context: This is the first step of Darwin's Jar. You make sea-strength salt water, check which kitchen seeds float, and start soaking moong seeds.

flow.do: 1. Pour away the water from both tumblers. 2. Rinse each lot of seeds three times in fresh water. 3. Spread each lot on a damp cloth on a plate. Label the plates. 4. Look closely at both lots and write what you notice.
flow.say: Rinse both lots well. Look at them side by side. Do the two lots look the same? What is different?
flow.kid: Pour the water away. Rinse both lots three times. Put each lot on a damp cloth. Label the plates. Do they look the same?

ask.q: Which lot of seeds has swollen more? Why might that be?
good: The plain water lot is fatter.
Perhaps salt water does not go into a seed so easily.

flow.parent: The seeds from plain water are usually much more swollen. Water moves into a seed less easily from salt water. Keep both cloths damp but not flooded. Keep the plates out of direct sun.
flow.context: In this step of Darwin's Jar you rinse the soaked moong seeds and set both lots on damp cloths.

flow.do: 1. Count the seeds in each lot that have a root showing. 2. Write both numbers. 3. Sprinkle water on both cloths.
flow.say: Count the seeds with a root showing in each lot. Which lot is ahead?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a root in each lot. Write the numbers. Sprinkle water on both cloths.
flow.context: In this step of Darwin's Jar you count the sprouted seeds on day 3.

flow.do: 1. Count the sprouted seeds in each lot again. 2. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 3. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: Count once more. Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Did the sea water kill the seeds?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts again. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Did the salt water kill the seeds?

ask.q: Moong seeds sink. So even if they live through sea water, could moong cross a sea alone? What else would a seed need?
good: No, they would sink to the bottom.
The seed would need to float, or ride on something that floats.

flow.parent: We expect that many of the salt water seeds still sprout, often a day later than the others. But this test has not been tried in every kitchen, so write down what you really find. If none of the salt lot sprout, that is a real result too. Darwin soaked seeds for 28 days, and most kinds still sprouted. He then met the same problem as you: most seeds sink. So he tried whole dried branches with ripe fruits, and many of those floated for weeks.
flow.think: Darwin's friends were sure that sea water kills seeds. Nobody had tried it. What else do people say that nobody has tested?
flow.context: This is the last step of Darwin's Jar. You compare the two lots and say whether a day in sea water killed the seeds.

activities.title: Read the Shape: how would these kitchen seeds travel with no person to carry them?
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at five or six fruits and seeds from the kitchen. From the shape, weight and covering of each one, you work out how the seeds would leave the parent plant if no person carried them. Three quick tests help: a drop, a float and a cling.

materials.item: drumstick, as fresh or as ripe as you can find
coconut with some husk still on, or a piece of husk, or a coir scrubber
ripe tomato or a ripe red chilli
tamarind pod, or a piece of tamarind with the seeds in
groundnuts in the shell
ball of cotton wool or a cotton wick, if you have one
tumbler of water and a steel plate
knife, for a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Wash hands after touching the chilli, and keep fingers away from eyes.
activities.record: Make a table with five columns: the fruit or seed, my guess, the drop test, the float test, and how I now think the seeds travel. Draw the drumstick seed with the wings.

example_chart.title: What the shape of each kitchen fruit shows
cols: How the seeds most likely travel
rows: Three papery wings round a small seed
Waterproof skin, and a thick husk with air in it
Soft, bright flesh round many small hard seeds
Inside an animal who eats the fruit. For chilli, a bird
Sweet and sour pulp round very hard seeds, in a pod that stays shut
Inside monkeys and other large fruit-eaters
A plain pod that ripened under the soil
Long hairs growing from the seed coat
Wind and water, scientists think, for wild cotton
example_chart.show: Six fruits and seeds from an Indian kitchen, with the feature to look for and the way each kind of seed most likely leaves the parent plant.
example_chart.note: All six are crops. Today people carry and sow nearly all of their seeds. The shapes show how their wild ancestors travelled.

setup.art: A steel plate holding a drumstick, a piece of coconut husk, a tomato, a tamarind pod, two groundnuts in the shell and a ball of cotton.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the fruits and seeds. Guess how each one travels, and say why.

setup.art: A drumstick cut open along its length, showing a row of round seeds, each with three thin pale wings.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts each one open. Look at the seeds and what is round them.

setup.art: A child dropping a winged drumstick seed from above their head with one hand, beside a tumbler of water with a piece of coconut husk floating in it.
setup.caption: 3. Do the three tests: drop each one, float each one, and rub each one on your sleeve.

flow.do: 1. Lay the fruits and seeds on a plate. 2. Your child looks at each one closely, without cutting. 3. Ask the questions below and write each guess with its reason.
flow.say: No plant can walk. Imagine no person carries these seeds. How would each one get away from the parent plant? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Look at each fruit closely. No person will carry these seeds. How would each one travel? Say what makes you think so.

ask.q: Which of these do you think the wind could carry? What would a wind seed need?
good: None of them, they are all too heavy.
A wind seed would need to be very light.
It would need a wing or fluff.

flow.parent: Take any guess that comes with a reason. Children often say none of these can go by wind, because the whole fruits are heavy. The drumstick seed inside will surprise them.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Shape. You look at kitchen fruits and guess how the seeds of each would travel.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts open the drumstick, the tomato or chilli, and the tamarind. Shell one groundnut. 2. For each seed or fruit, do three tests. Drop each one from above your head and watch the fall. Put each one in the tumbler of water. Rub each one on a sleeve and see what clings. 3. Write what you see.
flow.say: Look at what is round each seed. Now test each one. Which fall slowly? Which float? Which cling to cloth?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts each one open. Look at the seeds. Drop each one. Float each one. Rub each one on your sleeve. Write what you see.

ask.q: The drumstick seed has three thin wings. What do you think they are for?
good: To catch the wind.
To make the seed fall slowly.

flow.parent: In a young cooking drumstick the wings are soft, white and damp, and the seed will not fall slowly. Dry one seed in the sun for a day and try again. In a ripe brown pod the wings are papery. Coconut husk and groundnut shells float. Tamarind seeds and tomato seeds sink.
flow.context: In this step of Read the Shape you open each fruit and test how the seeds fall, float and cling.

flow.do: 1. Compare the test results with the first guesses. 2. Look at the table of what each shape shows. 3. Ask the questions below and the check question.
flow.say: Which guesses do you still agree with? Which have you changed? What was your evidence?
flow.kid: Look at your guesses again. Which ones would you change now? Say what you saw that changed your mind.

ask.q: The groundnut ripened under the soil, beside the parent. Is that a bad plan for a plant? Why, or why not?
good: The seeds are hidden from birds.
The place was good enough for the parent.
It could be bad, because the young are crowded.

ask.q: All of these are crops. Who carries their seeds today?
good: People.
Farmers and shopkeepers, and us.

check.q: A seed is small and light, with a thin papery wing. What is the best evidence that the wind carries seeds like this?
options: The seed falls slowly when dropped
The seed is brown
The seed has a hard coat
check.why: A slow fall gives the wind time to carry the seed sideways. Colour and a hard coat do not help a seed stay in the air. Choosing them means looking at the seed but not at what the wing does.

flow.parent: The shape is good evidence, but it is not proof. Scientists check by watching what really happens to the seeds. The groundnut shows that not every plant sends the seeds far.
flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Shape. You compare your guesses with what the tests showed.

activities.title: The Curl Test: how can a dry pod throw seeds with no muscles?
activities.context: In this activity you find out how a pod can move by drying. First you wet one side of a paper strip and watch the strip curl. Then you leave empty pod halves from the kitchen in the sun for two days and see what shape they take.

materials.item: strips of notebook paper, each about 10 centimetres long and 1 centimetre wide
saucer of water
fresh pods of peas, flat beans, cluster beans or French beans
sunny windowsill and a plate

schedule.what: Do the paper strip test. Split the pods, take out the seeds, draw one pod half, and put the halves on a sunny windowsill.
Look at the dried pod halves. Draw one again and compare the two drawings.

activities.record: Draw a paper strip before and after wetting, and mark the wet side. Draw one pod half on day 1 and the same half on day 3. Write one sentence saying what drying did to the shape.

setup.art: A hand laying a thin strip of paper flat on the surface of water in a saucer, and a second strip beside it already curled into a hoop.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a paper strip flat on water. Watch what the strip does in the first ten seconds.

setup.art: Four green pods split into halves with the seeds taken out, lying on a plate on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 2. Split the pods, take out the seeds, and leave the empty halves in the sun.

setup.art: Dry brown pod halves on a plate, several of them twisted into loose spirals.
setup.caption: 3. After two days, look at the shape of the dry halves.

flow.do: 1. Ask what will happen when a paper strip is laid flat on water. Write the guess and the reason. 2. Lay one strip gently on the water, so that only the lower side gets wet. 3. Watch for ten seconds. 4. Do it again with a new strip.
flow.say: What will this strip do when one side gets wet? Why do you think so? Now lay it flat on the water and watch.
flow.kid: Guess what a paper strip will do on water. Say why. Lay the strip flat on the water. Watch for ten seconds.

ask.q: The strip curled up off the water. Which side got longer, the wet side or the dry side?
good: The wet side. It is on the outside of the curve.
The wet side swelled.

flow.parent: The strip curls upward within a few seconds. Paper fibres swell when wet, so the wet side grows a little longer than the dry side. A strip with one long side and one short side has to bend. After a minute the water soaks through, and the strip goes flat again.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Curl Test. You wet one side of a paper strip and watch the strip curl.

flow.do: 1. Split each pod along the seam and take out the seeds. 2. Your child draws one pod half. 3. Ask what shape the halves will have when they are dry, and why. 4. Put the halves on a plate on a sunny windowsill.
flow.say: A pod wall has layers, like the two sides of the paper strip. What will happen to these halves as they dry? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Split the pods. Take out the seeds. Draw one pod half. Guess what shape the halves will have when dry. Put them in the sun.

ask.q: If one layer of the pod wall shrinks more than the other as it dries, what must the wall do?
good: Bend or curl, like the paper.
Twist.

flow.parent: The seeds can go into dinner. Do not explain yet what will happen.
flow.wait: Leave the pod halves in the sun for 2 days
flow.context: In this step of the Curl Test you put empty pod halves in the sun and predict what shape they will dry into.

flow.do: 1. Look at the dry halves. 2. Your child draws the same half again. 3. Ask what they see and why they think it happened. Then read the note below together.
flow.say: What shape are the halves now? Why do you think a flat pod wall dried into that shape?
flow.kid: Look at the dry pod halves. Draw one again. What changed? Say why you think that happened.

ask.q: On the plant, the two halves are joined along a seam while they dry. What happens when the seam finally gives way?
good: The halves spring apart and twist.
The seeds are flicked out.

check.q: A dry pod bursts and throws the seeds. Where did the energy for the throw come from?
options: Strain built up as the pod dried
Muscles in the pod wall
The seeds pushing outwards
check.why: As the pod dries, the layers of the wall shrink by different amounts. The wall wants to twist but the seam holds it flat, like a bent spring. When the seam breaks, the stored energy flings the seeds. Choosing 'muscles' gives a plant an animal's way of moving.

flow.parent: Many pod halves twist into a loose spiral, and some only curl a little. Write down what yours did. The wall of a bean pod has two layers of stiff fibres that lie at a slant to each other. As they dry, each layer shrinks in a different direction, so the wall twists. Shop beans may twist less than wild ones. For thousands of years farmers have chosen plants whose pods stay shut, so that the seeds do not spill before the harvest.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Curl Test. You see what shape the pod halves took as they dried.

activities.title: The Sock Walk: who rides on your feet? (if you have a park or a field nearby)
activities.context: In this activity you pull an old sock over one shoe and walk through rough grass at the edge of a park or a field. Then you pick off the seeds that have caught in the sock, and look at how each one holds on.

materials.item: old woollen or fluffy sock, big enough to pull over a shoe
hand lens, or a phone camera that can zoom
sheet of white paper and sticky tape
tweezers, if you have them

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along. Walk only in grass that is lower than your ankle, in a place you know well. Keep away from thorny bushes. Wash hands afterwards.
activities.record: Tape one seed of each kind onto the white paper. Beside each, draw the part that held on to the sock, as seen through the lens. Write how many kinds you found and how many seeds in all.

setup.art: A child's foot in a shoe with a large fluffy grey sock pulled over the shoe, at the edge of a patch of rough grass.
setup.caption: 1. Pull an old fluffy sock over one shoe.

setup.art: A child walking through ankle-high dry grass at the edge of a park, with small seeds stuck all over the sock.
setup.caption: 2. Walk fifty steps through rough, seeding grass.

setup.art: A sock laid on white paper with a child picking off seeds and a hand lens showing one seed with tiny hooks.
setup.caption: 3. Pick off the seeds. Look at how each one holds on.

flow.do: 1. Find a patch of rough grass that has gone to seed. 2. Ask the question below and write the guess. 3. Your child pulls the sock over one shoe.
flow.say: How many seeds do you think will ride on this sock after fifty steps? How could a seed hold on to wool?
flow.kid: Pull the sock over your shoe. Guess how many seeds will stick after fifty steps. How could a seed hold on?
flow.parent: The dry months after the rains are best, when grasses have ripe seeds. A mown lawn gives almost nothing. Try the rough edge of a park, a field path or an empty plot.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sock Walk. You guess how many seeds will catch on a sock in fifty steps.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks fifty steps through the grass, dragging the socked foot a little. 2. Take the sock off carefully, inside out, so that the seeds stay on. 3. Go home, or sit on a bench.
flow.say: Walk fifty steps and let your foot brush the grass. Then we take the sock off gently and look.
flow.kid: Walk fifty steps through the grass. Let your foot brush the plants. Take the sock off gently.
flow.context: In this step of the Sock Walk you walk through seeding grass with a sock over your shoe.

flow.do: 1. Turn the sock the right way out over the white paper. 2. Pick off every seed and sort them into kinds. 3. Look at one of each kind through the lens. 4. Count the kinds and the seeds.
flow.say: Sort the seeds into kinds. Look at each kind through the lens. What part of the seed was holding on?
flow.kid: Pick off the seeds. Sort them into kinds. Look at each through the lens. Find the part that held on. Count them.

ask.q: You carried these seeds away from the parent plants. Where would they have ended up if you had not picked them off?
good: Wherever the sock went next.
At home, or wherever they fell off.

ask.q: Which animals do this job when no child with a sock comes by?
good: Dogs, cows and goats.
Any animal with fur, and birds with feathers.

check.q: A seed has tiny hooks all over. What are the hooks most likely for?
options: Catching in an animal's fur
Floating on water
Falling slowly through the air
check.why: Hooks catch in fur, feathers and cloth, so a passing animal carries the seed away. Hooks add no air to help floating, and they are too small to slow a fall. Choosing those means matching the seed to the wrong carrier.

flow.parent: You may find spear grass with sharp points, burrs with hooks, and seeds with backward-pointing hairs. In 1941 a Swiss engineer, George de Mestral, looked at burrs from his dog's coat under a microscope. He copied their tiny hooks and invented Velcro. To go on, lay the sock in a tray of damp soil and see what comes up in two weeks.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Sock Walk. You sort the seeds from the sock and look at how each kind holds on.

activities.title: Where Did My Dinner Come From? Trace the journeys of ten foods
activities.context: In this activity you list ten plant foods from today's meals. You guess which of them first grew in India. Then you look up the home region of each one in a table, and count how many travelled here with people.

materials.item: notebook and pencil
the foods in today's meals, or the vegetable basket and the spice box
world map or globe, if you have one. A rough map drawn by hand will do

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: the food, my guess (India or elsewhere), and the home region from the table. Count the foods from each region. If you have a map, draw a line from each home region to where you live.

example_chart.title: Where some common Indian foods were first grown
rows: black pepper, cardamom, turmeric, mango, jackfruit, brinjal, cucumber, drumstick, curry leaf, sesame, moong, urad, tuvar
rice (also farmed very early in India), tea, soya bean, orange
West Asia and the lands round the Mediterranean Sea
wheat, chana, masoor, peas, coriander, cumin, methi, cabbage, cauliflower
ragi, jowar, bajra, tamarind, watermelon, coffee, cowpea
chilli, tomato, potato, maize, groundnut, rajma, pumpkin, capsicum, papaya, guava, cashew, pineapple, tapioca, cocoa
example_chart.show: Common foods of Indian kitchens, grouped by the part of the world where people first farmed each one.
example_chart.note: Coconut is left out, because coconuts spread across the Indian and Pacific Oceans by floating as well as with people. For a few crops, such as ginger and bhindi, scientists are still not sure of the first home.

setup.art: A child with a notebook looking into a vegetable basket and an open round steel spice box.
setup.caption: 1. List ten plant foods from today's meals.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list of foods and a tick or cross beside each under a heading 'From India?'.
setup.caption: 2. Guess for each one: did it first grow in India, or somewhere else?

setup.art: A hand-drawn outline map of the world with pencil lines running from South America, Africa and Central Asia to the tip of India.
setup.caption: 3. Look up each food in the table. Draw the journeys on a map.

flow.do: 1. Your child lists ten plant foods from today's meals. Include spices, dals and grains. 2. For each one they guess: first grown in India, or somewhere else? 3. Write the guesses and one reason.
flow.say: List ten plant foods we ate today. For each one, guess where people first grew it: in India, or somewhere else? Why?
flow.kid: List ten plant foods from today's meals. For each one, guess: from India first, or from somewhere else? Say why.

ask.q: Which three do you feel most sure are Indian? Why?
good: Chilli, because Indian food is spicy.
Rice, because we eat it every day.
Mango, because there are so many kinds here.

flow.parent: Most children, and most grown-ups, name chilli, tomato and potato as Indian. Do not correct the guesses yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did My Dinner Come From? You list ten plant foods and guess where each first grew.

flow.do: 1. Look up each food in the table of home regions. 2. Write the home region beside each guess. 3. Count the foods from each region. 4. On a map, draw a line from each region to your home.
flow.say: Find each food in the table. Where did it first grow? Count how many came from each part of the world.
flow.kid: Find each food in the table. Write the home region. Count the foods from each region. Draw the journeys on a map.

ask.q: Which food surprised you most? Why did you think it was from here?
good: Chilli, because it is in everything.
Tamarind, because it sounds so Indian.
Potato, because we eat it so often.

flow.parent: An example: idli and sambar. Rice, urad, tuvar, drumstick, turmeric and curry leaf are from Asia. Tamarind is from Africa. Onion is from Central Asia. Coriander is from the lands round the Mediterranean Sea. Tomato and chilli are from the Americas.
flow.context: In this step of Where Did My Dinner Come From? you look up the home region of each food and count the regions.

flow.do: 1. Ask how each plant could have made the journey. 2. Ask the questions below and the check question. 3. Your child writes one sentence about the most surprising journey.
flow.say: None of these plants can walk or swim. How did they cross oceans and mountains? Who carried them, and why?
flow.kid: These plants crossed oceans. How? Who carried them? Write one sentence about the journey that surprised you most.

ask.q: People carried chilli seeds on purpose. Name a plant that people carried without meaning to.
good: Weeds such as parthenium, in sacks of grain.
Seeds stuck to shoes, tyres and animals.

ask.q: The chilli has grown in India for 500 years. Is the chilli Indian now?
good: Yes, because Indian farmers made many new kinds here.
The chilli is both: from America, and Indian now.

check.q: Which of these did Indian cooks use to make food hot before the year 1500?
options: Black pepper
Chilli
Capsicum
check.why: Black pepper is a vine of the Western Ghats and has been used in India for thousands of years. Chilli and capsicum are the same kind of plant, and came from the Americas after 1498. Choosing chilli is very common, because chilli is now in almost every Indian dish.

flow.parent: There is no wrong answer to the last question. A plant can come from far away and still become part of a place.
flow.context: This is the last step of Where Did My Dinner Come From? You think about who carried each plant, and why.

activities.title: The Variety Count: how many kinds of rice, banana and mango does your family know?
activities.context: In this activity you count the varieties of three crops that your family knows by name. Then you ask an older person which varieties they ate as a child, and who saved the seeds. You find out whether any of those varieties have become hard to find.

materials.item: notebook and pencil
an older person to talk to: a grandparent, a neighbour, a farmer or a vegetable seller. A phone call is fine
rice, dal and fruit in the kitchen, to look at

activities.record: Write three lists: the varieties of rice, banana and mango that your family can name. Mark the ones the older person ate as a child. Circle any that are hard to find now. Make a card for one variety: the name, where it grows, and what is special about it.

setup.art: Three small heaps of different rice on a steel plate, with a child writing their names in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. List every variety of rice, banana and mango that your family can name.

setup.art: A girl sitting beside her grandmother on a step, holding a notebook and listening while the grandmother counts on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Ask an older person which varieties they ate as a child, and who kept the seeds.

setup.art: A hand-made card with a drawing of a red rice grain, a name and three short lines of writing.
setup.caption: 3. Make a card for one variety.

flow.do: 1. Look at the rice in the kitchen. Ask what kind it is. 2. Your child lists all the varieties of rice, banana and mango that the family can name. 3. Count each list.
flow.say: What kind of rice is this? How many kinds of rice can we name? How many kinds of banana? How many kinds of mango?
flow.kid: Find out what kind of rice is in the kitchen. List every kind of rice, banana and mango your family knows. Count each list.

ask.q: Two kinds of rice are both rice. So what is different about them?
good: The size, shape and colour of the grain.
The taste and the smell.
How long they take to grow, and what weather they can stand.

flow.parent: A variety is one kind within a crop. Ponni, sona masuri, basmati, matta and idli rice are varieties of rice. Poovan, nendran, rasthali and robusta are bananas. Banganapalli, alphonso, neelam and langra are mangoes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Variety Count. You list the varieties of rice, banana and mango that your family can name.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks an older person the four questions below. 2. They write the answers in a few words. 3. Thank the person.
flow.say: Ask these four questions. Which kinds did you eat as a child? Which are hard to find now? Who kept the seeds in your family? How were the seeds stored?
flow.kid: Ask an older person four things. Which kinds did you eat as a child? Which are hard to find now? Who saved the seeds? How did they keep them?
flow.parent: In many farming families the women chose and stored the seed. Seeds were often kept in clay pots or baskets with dry neem leaves or ash, sealed with clay. If the older person never farmed, ask about fruits and vegetables that tasted different when they were young.
flow.context: In this step of the Variety Count you ask an older person about the varieties they knew as a child.

flow.do: 1. Compare the older person's list with your child's list. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Your child makes a card for one variety.
flow.say: Which kinds did they know that we do not? Where have those kinds gone? Does it matter if a kind is lost?
flow.kid: Compare the two lists. Which kinds are missing from yours? Make a card for one variety. Write what makes that kind special.

ask.q: If farmers everywhere grew only one kind of rice, what could go wrong?
good: One disease could kill the whole crop.
That kind might not suit a flood or a dry year.
We would lose tastes, and rice for special uses.

check.q: Why do seed savers keep growing old varieties that give a smaller harvest?
options: They may resist a future disease or drought
Old seeds are always tastier
New varieties are not real plants
check.why: Each variety carries its own strengths, such as standing in flood water or resisting one disease. Nobody knows which strength will be needed next. Choosing 'always tastier' turns a reason about safety into a matter of taste.

flow.parent: Bananas are a useful example to mention. Most bananas sold across the world are one variety, called Cavendish, and a fungus disease is now spreading through those farms. India grows many banana varieties, which makes Indian banana farming safer.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Variety Count. You compare the two lists and make a card for one variety.

projects.title: Seed Keeper: save seeds from your kitchen, and test how many are alive
projects.context: In this 12-day project you become a seed saver. You take seeds from a ripe tomato, a dry red chilli and the spice box. You dry them, label them and store them. Then you test ten seeds of each kind on a damp cloth, to find out what share of them are alive.
projects.question: Are the seeds in an ordinary kitchen alive? What share of each kind will sprout?
projects.predict: You will put 10 seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. How many of each 10 do you think will sprout? Which kind will sprout first? Why do you think so? Write your numbers and your reasons.
projects.fair_test: Ten seeds of each kind lie on the same damp cloth, in the same place, for the same number of days. Ten is a small number, so treat the result as a rough guide. Seed banks test their seeds in the same way, with more seeds.

materials.item: fully ripe tomato
whole dry red chilli
methi, mustard or whole coriander from the spice box, one teaspoon
tea strainer
clean cotton cloth and a large plate
small paper envelopes, or squares of paper folded into packets
dry glass jar with a tight lid, and a spoonful of uncooked rice

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the tomato and opens the chillies. Wash hands with soap after touching chilli seeds, and keep fingers away from eyes.

schedule.what: Predict. Take out the tomato seeds and wash off the jelly. Shake out the chilli seeds. Spread all the seeds to dry in the shade.
Make three labelled packets. Put 10 seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. Store the rest in the jar.
Count the sprouted seeds of each kind. Keep the cloth damp.
Count again. Work out the percent alive for each kind. Write a conclusion.

projects.record: Write a label for each packet: the kind of seed, where the seed came from, and the date. Fill in the results table on day 7 and day 12. Work out the percent alive for each kind. Then write which packets you would keep for sowing, and why.

setup.art: A tea strainer held under a thin stream of water with tomato seeds in it, and a finger rubbing the seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Rub the tomato seeds in a strainer under water, to wash off the jelly.

setup.art: Three small heaps of seeds drying on a cloth in the shade: pale flat tomato seeds, round yellow chilli seeds and small brown methi seeds.
setup.caption: 2. Dry the seeds in the shade for two days.

setup.art: A plate with a damp cloth divided by pencil lines into three parts, with ten seeds in each part and a paper label beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Put 10 seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. This is the test of how many are alive.

setup.art: Three labelled paper packets going into a glass jar that has a layer of dry rice at the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Label the rest and store them in a dry jar with a spoonful of rice.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the tomato. Scoop the seeds into a tea strainer. Rub them under running water until the jelly is gone. 2. A grown-up breaks open the chillies. Shake the seeds onto paper. 3. Take a teaspoon of methi, mustard or coriander. Split each coriander ball gently into two halves. 4. Spread each kind on a cloth in the shade. 5. Ask for the predictions and the reasons.
flow.say: These seeds came out of our dinner. Are they alive? If we test 10 of each kind, how many will sprout? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Wash the jelly off the tomato seeds. Shake the seeds out of the chillies. Spread all the seeds to dry. Guess how many of each 10 will sprout. Say why.

ask.q: The chilli has been dry for months. The tomato is fresh. Which seeds are more likely to be alive? Why?
good: The tomato, because the fruit is fresh.
Both, because seeds are made to wait.
Perhaps not the chilli, if the chillies were dried with great heat.

flow.parent: The jelly round a tomato seed holds the seed back from sprouting inside the fruit, so wash it off well. A coriander ball is a fruit with two seeds, and sprouts better when split. Dry the seeds in shade, not in strong sun.
flow.wait: Let the seeds dry for 2 days
flow.context: This is the first step of Seed Keeper. You take seeds from a tomato, dry chillies and the spice box, and set them to dry.

flow.do: 1. Fold three paper packets. Write on each the kind of seed, where the seed came from, and the date. 2. Wet a cloth, squeeze it out, and lay it on a plate. 3. Put 10 seeds of each kind on the cloth, in three groups. Put a label beside each group. 4. Put the rest of the seeds in their packets. Put the packets in the jar with a spoonful of dry rice, and close the lid.
flow.say: A seed saver always labels. What must the label say? Now we set 10 of each kind on the damp cloth and store the rest.
flow.kid: Make three packets. Write the kind, the place and the date on each. Put 10 seeds of each kind on a damp cloth. Store the rest in the jar.

ask.q: Why do we keep the stored seeds dry, cool and dark?
good: Damp seeds would start to sprout or grow mould.
A dry seed stays alive much longer.

flow.parent: The dry rice takes up dampness from the air inside the jar. Keep the jar in a cupboard away from the stove. Keep the test cloth damp every day, and cover the plate with a second plate if the air is very dry.
flow.wait: Keep the cloth damp. Count in 4 days
flow.context: In this step of Seed Keeper you label the seeds, start the test on a damp cloth, and store the rest in a dry jar.

flow.do: 1. Count the seeds of each kind that have a root showing. 2. Write the numbers in the table. 3. Sprinkle water on the cloth.
flow.say: Count the seeds with a root in each group. Which kind sprouted first? Is that what you guessed?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a root in each group. Write the numbers. Which kind was first? Sprinkle water on the cloth.
flow.parent: Methi and mustard usually sprout in two or three days. Tomato takes five to eight days. Chilli and coriander are slow, and may show nothing yet.
flow.context: In this step of Seed Keeper you count the sprouted seeds on day 7.

flow.do: 1. Count the sprouted seeds of each kind again. 2. Work out the percent alive: multiply the number sprouted by 10. 3. Ask your child what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why. 4. Decide together which packets to keep.
flow.say: Count once more and work out the percent alive. Say what you thought would happen, and what you saw. Which packets would a seed saver keep?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts again. Multiply by 10 to get the percent alive. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Which packets would you keep?

ask.q: Suppose only 5 of your 10 chilli seeds sprouted. You want 10 chilli plants. How many seeds should you sow?
good: About 20, because only half are alive.

ask.q: Seed banks do this test on their seeds every few years. Why?
good: Stored seeds slowly die.
When too few sprout, the seeds must be grown again to make fresh seed.

flow.parent: Results differ a great deal from kitchen to kitchen. Some shop chillies are dried with heat, and few of their seeds live. Write down what you really find. One more thing that seed savers know: many shop tomatoes and chillies are hybrids, which means a cross between two different parent varieties. Their seeds sprout, but the plants that grow may not be like the parent fruit. Old varieties come true from seed, which is one reason seed savers keep them. Sow a few sprouts in a pot if you have one.
flow.think: A seed in your jar may wait a year. A seed in a seed bank may wait fifty. Who should decide when a stored seed gets to grow?
flow.context: This is the last step of Seed Keeper. You work out what share of each kind of seed is alive, and decide which to keep.

challenges.title: The Slow Fall Challenge: design a paper seed that takes the longest to fall 2 metres
challenges.context: This is a building challenge that follows the Fan Lane Test. In that test, the long-wing spinner fell slowest and travelled farthest. Now you design your own paper seed. It must carry one paper clip, and take as long as possible to fall 2 metres.
challenges.problem: From one small piece of paper, build a model seed that carries a paper clip and falls 2 metres as slowly as possible.
constraints: Use one piece of paper, 10 centimetres by 15 centimetres. That is about a quarter of a notebook page.
The model must carry one paper clip, which stands for the seed.
You may use scissors, 20 centimetres of sticky tape, and four pieces of thread, each 15 centimetres long.
The model is let go from 2 metres by opening the fingers. No throwing and no pushing.
materials: pieces of paper, 10 centimetres by 15 centimetres, three or four
general: A spinner with two wings, like the one in the Fan Lane Test, with the wings made longer or wider.
A parachute: a square of paper with a thread from each corner, and the paper clip hanging below.
A flat glider: a wide sheet with the paper clip at the front edge, so that the model slides forward as it sinks.
creative: A spinner with three wings, like a drumstick seed or the fruit of the hiptage vine.
A single curved wing with the paper clip at one end, like a mahogany seed.
A wide, thin wing swept back at the tips, like the gliding seed of the Javan cucumber vine.
A paper disc cut into a fringe of thin strips all round, like the hairs on a tridax fruit.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own paper seed and predict the fall time. Test it three times and find the mean. Did it beat the long-wing spinner? Then let it go in front of the fan. Did the slowest faller also travel farthest?

setup.art: A small rectangle of paper, a paper clip, a roll of tape, four short threads and scissors on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Start with one small piece of paper and one paper clip.

setup.art: Three paper models side by side: a two-winged spinner, a small square parachute on threads, and a flat glider with a clip at the front.
setup.caption: 2. Build a model seed that will fall as slowly as you can make it.

setup.art: A grown-up letting a paper model go from a mark high on a door frame while a child times the fall with a phone.
setup.caption: 3. Time three falls from 2 metres and find the mean.

flow.do: 1. Look up the long-wing spinner's mean fall time from the Fan Lane Test, or time it now. 2. Ask your child what makes a thing fall slowly. 3. Your child draws a design and writes a predicted fall time.
flow.say: The long-wing spinner took nearly 2 seconds to fall 2 metres. What made the fall slow? Draw a design that could be even slower. How long will yours take?
flow.kid: What makes a thing fall slowly? Draw your own paper seed. Guess how long your seed will take to fall 2 metres.

ask.q: You cannot change the weight of the paper clip. So what can you change?
good: How wide the paper spreads.
The shape, so that it spins or glides.
Where the clip sits.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow Fall Challenge. You plan a paper seed that will fall more slowly than the long-wing spinner.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the design. 2. Do one trial drop. 3. Your child changes one thing and tries again. 4. Allow three rounds of changes.
flow.say: Build it and try one drop. What did it do? Change one thing only, and try again.
flow.kid: Build your paper seed. Try one drop. Watch what happens. Change one thing. Try again.
flow.parent: Many first designs flip over or dive. A model is steady when the heavy clip is low and in the middle, or at the very front of a glider. Changing one thing at a time shows which change helped.
flow.context: In this step of the Slow Fall Challenge you build your paper seed and improve the design one change at a time.

flow.do: 1. Time three falls of the final design from 2 metres. 2. Work out the mean. 3. Compare it with the long-wing spinner. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Time three falls and find the mean. Did you beat the spinner? Which real seed is your design most like?
flow.kid: Time three falls. Find the mean. Did you beat the spinner? Which real seed is your design like?

ask.q: A slow fall is good for a wind seed. What would be the cost to a real plant of making a very big wing?
good: The wing takes food and material to make.
A big wing could catch in the branches.
The plant could make fewer seeds.

flow.parent: Engineers copy these shapes. Around 1905, Igo Etrich in Austria built gliders shaped like the gliding seed of the Javan cucumber vine. In 2021 and 2022, two teams in the United States built tiny sensors shaped like spinning seeds and dandelion fruits. The sensors are dropped from the air and drift down slowly over a wide area.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Slow Fall Challenge. You time your design and compare it with real seeds.

challenges.title: The Hitch-hiker Challenge: design a seed that rides on a sock, and gets off again
challenges.context: This is a building challenge about seeds that travel on the outside of animals. You build a model seed round one rajma bean. The model must catch on a woollen sock that brushes past, stay on for twenty steps, and still be able to come off.
challenges.problem: Build a model seed round a rajma bean that catches on a passing sock, stays on while you walk, and can be pulled off by one firm rub.
constraints: The rajma bean is the seed. The bean must stay whole and must be inside or on the model.
The model must be no longer than your thumb.
It must catch when a sock brushes past once. Nobody may press it on by hand.
It must stay on for 20 steps, and come off with one firm rub against a table leg.
materials: five bristles from a coconut-leaf broom, or five toothpicks
thread and a small piece of wool
general: Hooks: thin strips of paper or tape with the tips bent over, stuck all round the bean.
Spikes: broom bristles taped to the bean so that they point outwards.
Stickiness: a ring of tape round the bean with the sticky side facing out.
creative: Barbs that all point backwards, so that the seed slides into the wool easily but will not slide out.
A great many very small hooks in place of a few big ones, as on a burr.
A seed with sharp points on every side, so that one point always faces up, like the thorny fruit called nerunjil or gokhru.
A long springy tail that wraps round a thread of the sock.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own hitch-hiker and predict how many steps it will stay on. Test it. Then explain how your seed would get off the animal in the end. A seed that never comes off never reaches the soil.

setup.art: A red rajma bean on a table beside strips of paper, a roll of tape, five thin broom bristles and a fluffy sock.
setup.caption: 1. Start with one rajma bean. That bean is the seed.

setup.art: A model seed made of a bean wrapped in tape with many small bent paper hooks sticking out all round.
setup.caption: 2. Build hooks, spikes or stickiness round the bean.

setup.art: A child's foot in a fluffy sock brushing past a model seed lying on the floor, and the seed clinging to the sock.
setup.caption: 3. Brush a sock past once. Walk 20 steps. Is the seed still on?

flow.do: 1. Ask how a seed could hold on to fur with no hands. 2. Your child draws a design round a rajma bean. 3. They predict how many steps it will stay on.
flow.say: Some seeds travel on the fur of animals. How could a seed hold on? Draw your design. How many steps will it stay on?
flow.kid: How can a seed hold on to fur? Draw your design round a rajma bean. Guess how many steps it will stay on.

ask.q: Wool is made of many thin loops and hairs. What shape catches in a loop?
good: A hook.
A barb that points backwards.
Something sticky.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hitch-hiker Challenge. You plan a model seed that will cling to a sock.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds the model. 2. Lay it on the floor. Brush the socked foot past once. 3. If it catches, walk 20 steps. 4. Change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Build it and lay it on the floor. Brush your sock past once. Did it catch? Walk 20 steps. Change one thing and try again.
flow.kid: Build your seed. Put the seed on the floor. Brush your sock past once. Walk 20 steps. Change one thing and try again.
flow.parent: A grown-up handles the broom bristles and toothpicks if they are sharp. Most first models bounce off the sock. Smaller hooks, and more of them, usually work better than a few big ones.
flow.context: In this step of the Hitch-hiker Challenge you build your model and test whether the model rides on a sock.

flow.do: 1. Do the final test: one brush, 20 steps, then one firm rub on a table leg. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Your child writes one sentence on how the seed gets off.
flow.say: Final test. Did it catch, stay on, and come off again? In the wild, how would your seed leave the animal?
flow.kid: Do the final test. Did your seed catch? Did it stay on? Did it come off with one rub? Write how it would leave an animal.

ask.q: Why must a hitch-hiker seed be able to come off again?
good: If the seed stays on for ever, the seed never reaches the soil.
Animals rub and groom, and the seed must fall off then.

ask.q: The animal gets nothing for carrying a burr. How is that different from a bird who eats a berry?
good: The bird is paid with food.
The burr takes a free ride.

flow.parent: In 1941 the Swiss engineer George de Mestral found burrs in his dog's coat after a walk. Under a microscope he saw hundreds of tiny hooks. He spent years copying them in nylon, and the result was Velcro, which closes many shoes and bags today.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hitch-hiker Challenge. You test your model and explain how a real hitch-hiker would finally reach the soil.

items.p: Match each feature of a fruit or seed to the right carrier.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each feature solves one problem: staying in the air, staying afloat, being eaten, or holding on. A strong answer says what the feature does, as well as who carries the seed.
pairs: A thick husk full of air
A pod that curls as it dries

items.p: Why does a seedling often do badly right under the parent plant?
opts: The parent's leaves shade the ground
The soil there has no water at all
items.why: A seedling under the parent must share light, water and space with a much bigger plant. Enemies of that kind of plant also gather there. Choosing 'seeds need wind to sprout' mixes up travelling with sprouting.

items.p: The push of air against a moving thing is called air resistance, or ____.
a: drag
items.why: Drag pushes against anything that moves through air. It gets bigger as the thing goes faster and as the thing gets wider.

items.p: True or false: a winged seed pushes forward through the air with the wing.
items.why: False. A seed has no muscles and no engine. The wing slows the fall, and the wind carries the seed sideways. In still air a winged seed comes straight down.

items.p: Sort these by what usually carries them: wind, water or animals.
items.a: see items
items.why: Wings and hairs suit wind. Trapped air and a waterproof coat suit water. Flesh to eat, or hooks to cling, suit animals. A strong answer names the feature for one in each group.

items.p: Draw a paper spinner falling. Label: wing, paper clip, weight arrow, drag arrow, direction of spin.
a: Wing: the two flat blades at the top
Paper clip: at the bottom of the stem, standing for the seed
Weight arrow: points straight down
Drag arrow: points straight up, from the wings
Direction of spin: a curved arrow round the stem
items.why: A strong drawing shows the weight arrow and the drag arrow the same length, because at a steady fall speed the two are equal.
items.art: A blank outline of a two-winged paper spinner with a clip at the bottom, and five empty label lines.

items.p: In the Fan Lane Test, three fliers weigh the same. Which one usually lands farthest from the fan?
items.why: The long wings give the air the most to push on, so the fall is slowest and the wind carries that flier longest. Choosing 'all land together' means thinking that only weight matters.

items.p: A bulbul eats a berry. Put what happens to the seed in order.
a: The bulbul swallows the berry whole
The soft flesh is digested
The bulbul flies to another perch
The seed leaves in a dropping
The seed sprouts in a new place
items.why: The flesh is the bird's food, and the hard seed passes through whole. The flying in between is what moves the seed. A strong answer says why the seed is not digested.
items: The seed leaves in a dropping
The bulbul swallows the berry whole
The seed sprouts in a new place
The bulbul flies to another perch

items.p: The long-wing spinner and the packed strip weighed the same. Explain why the spinner landed farther from the fan.
items.a: The wings gave the air a wide surface to push on. So the spinner fell slowly, and the fan's wind had more time to carry the spinner sideways. The packed strip fell fast and reached the floor before the wind could move it far.
items.why: A strong answer says that the wind did the carrying, and that the wing only made the fall slower. It does not say that the wing pushed the spinner forward.

items.p: Three of these are carried by the wind. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Tridax and calotropis have hairs, and orchid seeds are as fine as dust, so wind carries all three. A coconut is far too heavy for wind, and floats on the sea.

items.p: True or false: most of the seeds of a tree land close to that tree.
items.why: True. Most seeds leave on an ordinary breeze, or simply drop. Only a few meet a strong gust, a flood or a far-flying animal. The pattern of landings is called the seed shadow.

items.p: A fruit on the plant is green, hard and sour. What does that tell an animal?
opts: The seeds are not ready yet
The fruit is poisonous for ever
items.why: An unripe fruit keeps eaters away until the seeds inside are ready to travel. Then the fruit turns soft, sweet and bright. Choosing 'poisonous for ever' misses that the same fruit will change when ripe.

items.p: Chilli, tomato and potato were carried to India by people from the ____.
a: Americas
America
South America
Central and South America
items.why: These crops were first farmed in Central and South America. Ships brought them to India after 1498.

items.p: Give two reasons why farmers should keep growing many varieties of one crop.
items.a: First, if a disease or pest attacks, some varieties may resist it, so not everything is lost. Second, different varieties suit different places and weather, such as floods, salty soil or dry years.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons. Taste, special uses and festivals are also good reasons.

items.p: What does a seed bank do?
opts: Keeps many kinds of seeds alive
Sells seeds at the lowest price
Turns old seeds into new kinds
items.why: A seed bank stores dry seeds, usually in the cold, so that they stay alive for decades. Choosing 'stops seeds from ever sprouting' misses the point: the seeds are kept so that they can be grown again.

items.p: Draw a tree from above. Add 20 dots to show where 20 of the tree's seeds land.
items.a: Most of the dots are close to the tree. A few are farther away, and one or two are far away, perhaps to one side where the wind blew.
items.why: A strong drawing does not spread the dots evenly. It shows many near and few far, which is the usual shape of a seed shadow.
items.art: A blank page with a small circle marked 'tree, seen from above' near one edge and an arrow marked 'wind'.

worksheets.title: Fall Speed, Far Trips and Farmed Seeds (stretch)

items.p: A seed falls for 10 seconds in a wind of 4 metres each second. How far sideways does the seed go?
items.why: Distance is about the time in the air multiplied by the wind speed. 10 × 4 = 40 metres. Choosing 14 means adding the numbers when they should be multiplied.

items.p: Half of a seed's wing is torn off. What happens to the fall speed and to the distance travelled? Say why.
items.a: The seed falls faster, because a smaller wing gives the air less to push on. So the seed spends less time in the air, and the wind carries the seed a shorter distance.
items.why: A strong answer links three things in a chain: less wing, faster fall, less time for the wind to carry.

items.p: Sort these: does it help a wind-carried seed go far, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: A wind seed goes far when the fall is slow, the start is high and the wind is strong. Extra weight makes the fall faster. A strong answer explains one from each group.
items: leaving on a calm, damp day

items.p: A falling seed stops speeding up when the drag is equal to the seed's ____.
a: weight
items.why: Weight pulls down and drag pushes up. When they are equal, they cancel, and the seed falls at a steady speed.

items.p: Why do birds eat hot chillies that mice and rats avoid?
opts: Birds do not sense the hot chemical
Chillies are only hot at night
items.why: The hot chemical, capsaicin, burns the mouths of mammals. Birds do not sense it. Birds also swallow the seeds whole, while mice chew them. Choosing 'birds like pain' gives the bird a feeling that the bird does not have here.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how wild rice became farmed paddy.
a: Wild rice drops ripe grains one by one
People gather the grains still on the stalks
People sow some of those grains
Each year more plants hold on to their grain
Farmed paddy holds every grain until threshed
items.why: Nobody planned the change. People could only harvest grains that had not fallen, so those were the ones that got sown. A strong answer says why the falling grains were left out.
items: People sow some of those grains
Farmed paddy holds every grain until threshed
Wild rice drops ripe grains one by one
Each year more plants hold on to their grain
People gather the grains still on the stalks

items.p: True or false: a coconut in the husk sinks in sea water.
items.why: False. The thick husk is full of air between the fibres, and the skin keeps water out. A coconut can float for more than three months.

items.p: The tuft of hairs on a dandelion fruit is mostly gaps. Why does the tuft still slow the fall so well?
opts: Air is slowed around every thin hair
The gaps are filled with glue
items.why: Air close to each thin hair is slowed down. The slowed air round one hair overlaps with that of the next, so the tuft acts almost like a solid disc. Choosing 'flap like wings' gives the fruit muscles.

items.p: A mangrove seed sprouts while still on the mother tree. How might that help in tidal mud?
items.a: The seedling drops with a root end ready to grow. So the seedling can take hold of the mud quickly, before the next tide washes the seedling away. A seedling that does not root can float off and try somewhere else.
items.why: A strong answer names the problem, which is that the tide moves everything twice a day, and then says how a ready-grown seedling solves that problem.

items.p: Three of these crops came to India from the Americas. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Black pepper is a vine of the Western Ghats and has grown in India for thousands of years. Chilli, tomato and potato came by ship after 1498.

items.p: Match each way of travelling to one risk that goes with it.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every way of travelling has a cost. A strong answer can add the gain for each one too, such as a long distance or a heap of manure.
pairs: most seeds land in a poor place
the seed may never reach land
the seed may be chewed and killed
the seed may never drop off
the seed goes only a few metres

items.p: The same spinner is let go 30 times in front of a fan. Why do the landings spread out?
opts: Moving air is never perfectly steady
The spinner gets heavier each time
The spinner aims at different spots
items.why: Even a fan gives small gusts and lulls, and no two releases are exactly alike. Outdoors the wind changes far more. Choosing 'aims' gives the paper a plan.

items.p: Acorns fall a few metres from an oak. Yet oaks once spread 1,000 kilometres in a few thousand years. Explain how.
items.a: A few acorns travel much farther than the rest. Birds such as jays carry acorns for kilometres and bury them, and forget some. Those rare long trips, repeated over many years, moved the oaks far faster than falling acorns could.
items.why: A strong answer says that the usual short trip cannot explain the spread, and that rare long trips can.

items.p: True or false: farmed maize can scatter seeds without any help from people.
items.why: False. The kernels are fixed to the cob, and the cob is wrapped in tight leaves. Unless someone opens the cob and sows the kernels, they have no way to spread.

items.p: A hill slope has burnt bare. Two people suggest how to bring the trees back.
items.a: A strong answer sees the trade-off. Planting fast foreign trees covers the soil quickly, but those trees may spread and crowd out local plants. Waiting for wind and birds brings the local plants back, but slowly, and rain may wash soil away in the meantime. Many foresters now plant or protect local trees first.
items.why: There is no single right answer. It depends on how steep the slope is, how close the nearest forest is, and how long people can wait.

views.says: Plant fast-growing trees from Australia now. In three years the slope will be covered, and the rain will not wash the soil away.
Keep the goats off and wait. The wind and the birds will bring seeds of our own trees from the next hill. It is slow, but it is our own forest that comes back.

items.ask: Which would you choose for a slope beside a forest? Which for a slope far from any forest? Give a reason for each, and one weakness of your choice.

items.p: Design a fruit for a plant that lives on a riverbank. Label the features that help the seeds travel by water.
items.a: The fruit has a light covering with air spaces, a waterproof skin and a tough coat round the seed. It may be shaped to float upright or to lodge in mud.
items.why: A strong drawing labels at least two features and says what each does: one for floating, and one for keeping the seed dry or safe.
items.art: A blank page with a simple riverbank and water drawn along the bottom.

items.p: Two people disagree about the best way to keep old rice varieties alive.
items.a: A strong answer sees that each way protects against a different danger. A cold seed bank protects against war, drought and neglect, and holds huge numbers. Growing in fields keeps the varieties changing with the weather and pests, and keeps the knowledge of how to grow and cook them. Most seed scientists and seed savers now say that both are needed.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The best answers name one thing that each way can do and the other cannot.

views.says: In our cold room, a packet of dry seed stays alive for fifty years. One building keeps safe more varieties than a thousand farms could.
A seed in a freezer learns nothing. My rice has met every flood and every pest of the last fifty years, and it is still here because I sow it.

items.ask: Which way would you trust with the last handful of a rare rice? Give your reason, and say what could go wrong with your choice.

items.p: The climate is warming. Should people carry the seeds of wild trees to cooler places?
items.a: A strong answer weighs the two risks against each other. If people do nothing, some trees may die out, because their seeds travel too slowly. If people move them, a tree may spread too well in the new place, or bring a disease with it. A careful answer may suggest moving trees only short distances, and watching them closely.
items.why: Scientists really do disagree about this. A good answer gives a reason and admits a risk.

views.says: This tree's seeds travel a few hundred metres in a lifetime. The climate that suits the tree is moving many kilometres. Without our help the tree will be left behind.

views.who: A scientist who studies invasive plants
views.says: Lantana was moved with good intentions too. We cannot test how a plant will behave in a new place until it is too late to take it back.

items.ask: Which side do you agree with more? Give one reason, and one thing that would change your mind.

items.p: You find a fruit covered in tiny hooks. Is that proof that animals carry it? How would you check?
items.a: No. The hooks are good evidence, but not proof. To check, I would watch the plant and see what happens to the fruits. I could look at the fur of animals that pass, or drag a cloth through the plants and see if the fruits catch.
items.why: A strong answer separates evidence from proof, and names a way to watch what really happens.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a higher start carry a spinner farther? Say what you change, keep and measure.
items.a: I change only the height of the start. I keep the same spinner, the same wind and the same way of letting go. I measure how far from the start mark the spinner lands, several times at each height. I need a wind that blows over the whole fall, such as a steady breeze outdoors, because a fan's wind is too narrow.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, repeats each drop, and notices that a fan cannot give wind over a tall drop.

items.p: With the same food, a plant can make 20 big seeds or 20,000 tiny ones. Which statement is true?
opts: The number of seeds never matters
items.why: A big seed gives a seedling a strong start in shade or dry soil, but few are made and they do not go far. Tiny seeds go far and are many, but each needs a perfect spot. Choosing 'always better' misses the cost on the other side.

items.p: A dandelion shuts the hairs in damp air and opens them in dry air. Is that deciding? Argue both sides.
items.a: For: the plant senses how damp the air is and acts differently because of it, which is what deciding means. Against: wet tissue swells and pulls the hairs shut, and some scientists say that the word 'decide' should be kept for animals with brains.
items.why: A strong answer gives both sides fairly and says what the argument turns on: what we mean by the word 'decide'.

items.p: Seed A falls at 1 metre each second and seed B at 4, from one tree. Which is true?
opts: A goes about 4 times as far
B goes about 4 times as far
A goes about 20 times as far
items.why: From a tree 20 metres tall, seed A is in the air for 20 seconds and seed B for 5 seconds. The wind carries A for four times as long, so A goes about four times as far. Choosing B means thinking that a faster fall is a faster journey.

items.p: True or false: one seed in ten thousand that travels very far is too rare to matter to a kind of plant.
items.why: False. A tree makes many thousands of seeds each year, so rare trips happen again and again. Those few seeds are how a kind of plant reaches new islands, new valleys and ground left bare by a fire.

items.p: Seedlings close to a parent tree of the same kind often die more than seedlings far away. What is one main reason?
opts: Enemies of that kind gather there
The parent tree poisons them on purpose
The ground near a tree is always dry
items.why: The enemies of one kind of plant are most common where that plant is common, which is round the parent. Seedlings there also get little light. Choosing 'poisons them on purpose' gives a reason that scientists have not found for most trees.

items.p: Match each observation to what it is evidence for.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A claim in science rests on something that someone saw or measured. A strong answer can say why each observation points to its claim and not to another.
pairs: With the fan off, a spinner lands at your feet
a wing gives no forward push
Wild relatives of chilli grow only in the Americas
Seeds sprout after four weeks in salt water
seeds could cross a sea alive
Trays near a tree catch the most seeds
most seeds land near the parent

items.p: Sort these: is it settled, or do scientists still argue about it?
items.a: see items
items.why: Science has both. A strong answer can say what kind of evidence would be needed to settle one of the open ones.
items: Many seeds survive an animal's gut
Whether a plant's timing counts as deciding
Whether to move trees to cooler places
Whether giant animals now gone shaped some fruits

items.p: Farmed paddy no longer scatters grain. For the paddy plant, is that a loss or a gain? Give your reason.
items.a: It can be argued both ways. It is a loss, because paddy now depends wholly on people and would die out without them. It is a gain, because people sow paddy on a huge part of the Earth's land, and there are far more paddy plants than there ever were wild rice plants.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side or holds both, and gives a reason drawn from what the plant gets and what the plant gives up.

items.p: Draw the bar chart you expect for a real tree's seed shadow, from 0 to 500 metres. Mark the far seeds.
items.a: The bars are tall near 0 metres and drop quickly. Beyond about 100 metres the bars are very low, but they do not reach zero. A few seeds are marked far to the right.
items.why: A strong drawing has a long, low tail to the right. It marks that tail as the part that is hardest to measure and matters most for reaching new places.
items.art: A blank pair of axes, with 'distance from the tree (metres)' along the bottom from 0 to 500 and 'number of seeds' up the side.

items.p: Lantana was brought to India as a garden flower and now covers forests. What does this show about moving plants?
opts: A moved plant can behave in unexpected ways
Birds refuse to eat foreign berries
items.why: Lantana found birds to carry the berries and few enemies to eat the leaves. Nobody expected that. But chilli and tomato were moved too, and did no such harm. Choosing 'every foreign plant is harmful' goes further than the evidence.

items.p: A seed takes 30 seconds to fall. The wind blows at 3 metres each second. How far does the seed go?
items.a: The seed goes 30 × 3 = 90 metres. Now suppose rising air holds the seed up for one minute more. That adds 60 × 3 = 180 metres, and the total is 270 metres, three times as far.
items.why: A strong answer multiplies the time by the wind speed. A very strong answer adds that anything which keeps the seed up longer, such as rising air, adds a great deal of distance.

items.p: True or false: the shape of a fruit is proof of how the seeds travel.
items.why: False. A shape is good evidence, but scientists check by watching what really happens. Some fruits travel in two ways, and some shapes may have suited animals who are no longer alive.

quiz.p: Which of these is a reason why a seed often does better away from the parent?
opts: Less competition for light and water
quiz.why: Away from the parent, a seedling shares light, water and space with fewer plants of the same kind, and meets fewer of their enemies. Far soil is not always richer. Most seeds that travel land somewhere poor.

quiz.p: A fruit has a waterproof skin and a thick, light husk full of air. How do the seeds most likely travel?
quiz.why: Trapped air makes the fruit float, and the waterproof skin keeps the seed dry. That is the coconut's design. The fruit is far too heavy for wind.

quiz.p: A seed carries a small oily food parcel on the outside. Who most likely carries this seed?
quiz.why: Ants carry the whole seed to the nest, eat the parcel, and leave the seed in their rubbish heap. The parcel is too small to pay a large animal.

quiz.p: Two seeds weigh the same, and one has a wing. Why does the winged seed fall more slowly?
opts: The wing meets more air resistance
The wing makes the seed lighter
Gravity pulls the winged seed less
quiz.why: The wing adds surface and almost no weight. With more surface, drag matches the weight at a lower speed. Gravity pulls both seeds equally, because they weigh the same.

quiz.p: True or false: a falling seed keeps getting faster all the way to the ground.
quiz.why: False. Drag grows as the speed grows. When drag equals weight, the seed stops speeding up and falls at a steady speed. A winged seed reaches that speed within a metre or two.

quiz.p: On a day with no wind at all, where does a winged seed from a tall tree land?
opts: Far away, because of the wing
quiz.why: A wing gives no forward push. With no moving air, the seed only comes down slowly. Choosing 'far away' treats the wing as an engine.

quiz.p: Which change would carry a winged seed the farthest?
opts: A higher start in a stronger wind
quiz.why: Distance is about the time in the air multiplied by the wind speed. A higher start gives more time, and a stronger wind gives more speed. A heavier seed or a shorter wing makes the fall faster.

quiz.p: In a wind test, why do you let each flier go five times and take the mean?
opts: One drop could be a fluke
