The paper needs to warm up
The fan tires after one drop
quiz.why: Moving air is never perfectly steady, so single drops differ. The mean of several drops is a fairer picture than any one of them.

quiz.p: Which of these describes a seed shadow?
opts: Many seeds near, and a few far away
Seeds that grow only in the dark
The same number of seeds at every distance
quiz.why: A seed shadow is the pattern of where a plant's seeds land. Most land near, and a few go far. Those few are how plants reach new places.

quiz.p: Which of these shows that a crop has come to depend on people?
opts: Paddy holds the grain until threshed
quiz.why: Wild rice drops ripe grains. Farmed paddy holds them, so the grain is sown only when a person sows it. Coconuts and tridax still travel without us.

quiz.p: Which of these foods was carried to India from the Americas?
quiz.why: Tomato was first farmed in Central and South America and came to India by ship after 1498. Mango, pepper and turmeric are from South Asia.

quiz.p: Why is a field planted with one single variety risky?
opts: One disease could kill the whole crop
The seeds forget how to sprout
quiz.why: Plants of one variety are nearly the same as each other. A disease that can attack one can attack them all. With many varieties, some are likely to resist.

quiz.p: True or false: seeds kept in a cold seed bank go on changing to suit the weather outside.
quiz.why: False. Seeds in a cold store stay as they were when they went in. Only plants that are grown year after year can change with the weather and pests. That is why many people say both ways of saving are needed.

applications: Foresters collect winged seeds in the dry season and sow them on bare slopes, timing the work to the winds and the first rains.
Engineers have built tiny sensors shaped like spinning seeds and dandelion fruits. Dropped from the air, they drift down slowly and spread over a wide area.
Velcro, the fastener on shoes and bags, copies the tiny hooks of a burr.
Early glider builders copied the wide, swept-back wing of the gliding seed of the Javan cucumber vine.
Plant inspectors at ports and airports check grain, soil and luggage, to stop the seeds of new weeds from entering a country.
Seed banks send stored seeds to farmers and plant breeders when a new disease appears, so that resistant varieties can be found.
Conservation teams protect hornbills, fruit bats and elephants partly because many forest trees depend on them to carry seeds.
Mangrove planters along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Bengal collect floating seedlings and push them into the mud, to protect the shore from storms.

open_questions.q: How far do seeds really travel?
open_questions.why_open: The seeds that go farthest are the rarest, perhaps one in many thousands. They are almost impossible to find. So the most important part of a seed shadow is the part scientists can measure least well.

open_questions.q: Can trees move fast enough to keep up with a warming climate?
open_questions.why_open: The places that suit each tree are shifting by kilometres in a human lifetime. Nobody knows which trees can keep up through rare long trips, and which will be left behind.

open_questions.q: How does a plant sense that the wind is right for letting seeds go?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that many plants release seeds mostly in dry gusts. For most plants they do not yet know which part senses the dryness and the pull, or how.

open_questions.q: Which fruits were shaped by animals who are no longer alive?
open_questions.why_open: Some large fruits have no carrier today. They may have been eaten by giant animals who died out thousands of years ago. It is very hard to test what those animals ate.

open_questions.q: How many seeds do people carry by accident every day?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds ride on tyres, shoes, clothes, ships and aeroplanes. A few studies have counted seeds in road tunnels and on boots, but nobody knows the total for the world.

maths.problem: In one Fan Lane Test, the long-wing spinner landed 150, 190, 160, 210 and 140 centimetres from the start mark. What was the mean distance?
maths.explain: Add the five distances: 150 + 190 + 160 + 210 + 140 = 850. Divide by the number of drops: 850 ÷ 5 = 170 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Fan Lane Test, you let each paper flier go five times in front of a fan and measure how far away each drop lands.
maths.why_maths: Five drops give five different distances. The mean turns them into one fair number that you can compare with another flier.

maths.problem: In the same test, the long-wing spinner's mean distance was 170 centimetres and the packed strip's was 25 centimetres. About how many times as far did the spinner go?
maths.explain: 170 ÷ 25 = 6.8, which is close to 7. Both fliers weighed the same, so the shape alone made the spinner travel about 7 times as far.
maths.context: In the Fan Lane Test, a packed strip and a long-wing spinner of the same weight are let go in the same wind.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'about 7 times as far' shows how much difference a wing makes, more clearly than two separate numbers do.

maths.problem: A winged seed leaves the top of a tree 25 metres tall and falls at a steady 1 metre each second. The wind blows at 4 metres each second. About how far from the tree does the seed land?
maths.explain: The fall takes 25 ÷ 1 = 25 seconds. In each second the wind carries the seed 4 metres. 25 × 4 = 100 metres.
maths.context: In the Fan Lane Test, you found that the wind carries a flier only while the flier is in the air.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying time by speed lets you predict a seed's journey from a real tree, which no fan at home can test.

maths.problem: Seed A falls at 1 metre each second and seed B at 5 metres each second. Both leave a branch 20 metres up, in a wind of 3 metres each second. How much farther does seed A travel?
maths.explain: Seed A falls for 20 ÷ 1 = 20 seconds and travels 20 × 3 = 60 metres. Seed B falls for 20 ÷ 5 = 4 seconds and travels 4 × 3 = 12 metres. 60 − 12 = 48 metres. Seed A goes 5 times as far, because the fall lasts 5 times as long.
maths.context: In the Fan Lane Test, the flier that fell slowest in still air also travelled farthest in the wind.
maths.why_maths: Working out both journeys shows that the distance depends on the fall time, not on any push from the seed.

maths.problem: In a Seed Shadow Test, 2 of 30 drops landed beyond 2 metres. A real tree makes 15,000 seeds. If the same share went beyond the usual distance, how many seeds would that be?
maths.explain: 2 out of 30 is the same as 1 out of 15. 15,000 ÷ 15 = 1,000. So a share that looks tiny in 30 drops becomes a thousand seeds for a real tree.
maths.context: In the Seed Shadow Test, you let the same paper spinner go 30 times and tally how far away each drop lands.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a fraction up shows why rare far trips matter: rare for one seed is common for a tree with thousands.

maths.problem: Charles Darwin soaked the seeds of 87 kinds of plants in salt water for 28 days. Seeds of 64 kinds still sprouted. What percent of the kinds survived?
maths.explain: 64 ÷ 87 = 0.735 and a little more. As a percent that is about 74. So nearly three kinds in every four survived four weeks in sea water.
maths.context: In Darwin's Jar, you soak moong seeds in salt water for a day and count how many still sprout, as Darwin did in 1855.
maths.why_maths: A percent lets you compare Darwin's result with your own, though he tested 87 kinds of plants and you tested 10 seeds.

maths.problem: A coconut can float for 110 days and still sprout. A sea current carries it at 1 kilometre each hour. How far could it go? The Lakshadweep islands are about 400 kilometres from Kochi. Is that within reach?
maths.answer: About 2,640 kilometres. Yes, Lakshadweep is well within reach.
maths.explain: In one day the current carries the coconut 24 × 1 = 24 kilometres. In 110 days that is 110 × 24 = 2,640 kilometres. That is more than six times the distance from Kochi to Lakshadweep.
maths.context: In Darwin's Jar, you checked which kitchen seeds and fruits float in salt water. A coconut in the husk is one of the best floaters of all.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying speed by time shows that a slow current is enough to carry a floating seed across a sea.

maths.problem: In Seed Keeper, 7 of your 10 tomato seeds sprouted. You want 21 tomato plants. About how many seeds should you sow?
maths.explain: 7 out of 10 seeds are alive. To get 21 plants you need 3 lots of 7, because 21 ÷ 7 = 3. So you sow 3 lots of 10, which is 30 seeds.
maths.context: In Seed Keeper, you test 10 seeds of each kind on a damp cloth to find out what share of them are alive.
maths.why_maths: Farmers and seed banks use this sum every season, to decide how thickly to sow seed that is not all alive.

playtest: Read through step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but have not been tried at home. Please treat the expected results as likely and not certain. The Fan Lane Test needs a table fan or a pedestal fan, and about 3 metres of clear floor. A ceiling fan will not do, and must be switched off. Homes without a standing fan can use an air cooler, or a hair dryer on the cool setting held steady by a grown-up. The three fliers must come from the same sheet and carry the same size of paper clip, or the test is not fair. A spinner that will not spin nearly always has both wings folded the same way. Fold one wing forward and one back. If neither spinner spins, add a second clip to all three fliers. The packed strip falls 2 metres in about 0.6 seconds, which is too quick to time well by hand. That is fine, because the gap between it and the spinners is large. In the fan's wind a spinner may tumble before spinning. Count every drop. Distances depend on the fan, so the example numbers are only a guide. The Seed Shadow Test takes 30 drops and about ten minutes. A steady fan gives a narrow pattern, and the fan turning from side to side gives a wider one. Darwin's Jar uses one and a half level teaspoons of salt in a 200 millilitre tumbler. We expect many salt-soaked moong to sprout a day late, but this has not been checked in a kitchen, so any result should be written down as found. In Read the Shape, the wings of a young cooking drumstick seed are soft and damp. Dry one seed for a day before the drop test. Coconut husk can be replaced by a coir scrubber. In the Curl Test, the paper strip curls within seconds. The pod halves may twist strongly or only a little, because shop beans were bred to stay shut. The Sock Walk needs rough grass with ripe seeds, and is marked for families with a park or field nearby. It is not part of the core path. Each of the 16 clue cards was checked against the unit's own explanations. The story is about 1,100 words and takes about 12 minutes to read aloud. The three films have no confirmed addresses yet.
